texto: I was not a fan of this one. I respect its place in cinematic history, but I found it underwhelming and disappointing. I’m cool with long runtimes, but this feels indulgent, tiresome, and tedious in a way that Yi Yi never does. The pacing feels flat, and the film overall feels dull and quite boring. Fanny & Alexander by Bergman is 5 hours long, 1 hour longer than ABSD, and it does not feel this tedious. I’m cool with slice of life movies, I’m cool with movies that wander, as long as I care about the characters and feel engaged. But it felt very unfocused. I’m not left caring deeply about anyone or anything in particular. The characters didn’t feel very fleshed out or developed. The film stuffs so many characters in one that it’s hard to truly connect with anybody. Also, some of Yang’s weakest writing for his female characters. Not as egregious as Mahjong, but the women here are bland afterthoughts. Disappointing compared to the fullness of his female characters in A Confucian Confusion and That Day, On the Beach. Overall, the film’s size doesn’t match the size of emotion and connection that it elicits. It’s an investment with minimal returns.

tema: Fotografia e direção de arte elogiados, mas não bastam
exemplo: Apesar de algumas críticas reconhecerem a qualidade da fotografia, da direção de arte e do estilo visual do filme, elas afirmam que isso não é suficiente para compensar o ritmo lento e a falta de envolvimento com a história.
texto: My first Edward Yang film, and while the story itself is relatively clear about Taiwan’s situation during the period it portrays, the aftermath of the Chinese Civil War, the migration to the island, and the way violence, prejudice, and social tensions shaped that society, the way the film chooses to tell all of this feels far more fragmented and disorienting. At first, it seems as though we will follow a single character in something close to a coming-of-age story, especially through his feelings for a girl. But over the course of its four-hour runtime, the film constantly branches out into teenage power disputes, gang rivalries, side characters, and parallel stories that do not always clearly converge with the main narrative. This also extends to Yang ’s mise-en-scène. Many of the film’s most important moments avoid the traditional shot-reverse-shot structure; the camera often remains static, refusing to follow reactions or decisive actions, leaving much of what happens outside the frame, almost as mere suggestion. It’s an interesting style because it forces the viewer to fill in the gaps through their own perception, yet at the same time it dissipates some of the dramatic weight of the events and weakens the emotional involvement with what the characters are going through.

texto: I don't really feel like going along with the delusion that this isn’t just unnecessarily long. Given the brief synopsis, I expected a 4-hour run time to give us a plethora of experiences. Instead, we get repetition. Repetition and repetition. Extraordinarily little character growth and slow, ultimately meaningless expansion on the same few themes. It's well made. You are drawn in by the emotion. If you are looking for more of an experience than a movie, then, yes, this is up in that 4+ star range it seems overstuffed with. The point is the grinding, slow despair and after 4 hours you are one with the characters. I don't think 4 hours were needed to make the ending impactful. Many movies can do the same in less than 2. I'm just not here for that experience and the story itself could be effortless wrapped up in 90-120 minutes. There are multiple storylines that are completely unnecessary in any reasonable interpretation of the story, such as the filmmaking one. I didn't dislike this and the run time didn't elicit any negative reaction, probably because I watched it over quite a few installments. I just think, again, there was so much that is unnecessary. I won't say self-indulgent, because I don't think that's what they were going for, I think it's to draw you in to what the filmmakers and characters lives were like, as I said. An OK, but not enthusiasic rating from me.

texto: Wanted to connect with this the way I did with Yi Yi , but alas. Regardless, it’s a thorough restoration from Criterion that does justice to Yang’s vision. The guy was a creative visionary, no doubt about it. This epic pushes 4 hours with a focus on the lives of the Taiwanese children of Chinese expats/refugees fleeing mainland China after the Civil War. Though one could be mistaken in thinking the gang ‘turf war’ is only nominally a “war”, Yang disabuses us of that notion as he captures dramatic scenes of street violence, targeted hits on youth leaders and juvenile delinquency of all forms. The kids are abused and neglected at home, and they re-assert familiar power structures in the *playgrounds (*the tennis court, the music hall, the restaurant). Yang’s only music comes in diegetic form via ‘50s Western rock ‘n roll hits and sappy love ballads from Ricky Nelson to Elvis whom the characters adore. It’s a tapestry of a specific place during a specific moment in time under unique political circumstances, but for me, Yang seems unable to bridge the knowledge gap with the audience enough to make me care, especially given this runs at a punishingly languid pace.

texto: My hot take? This is Burning but worse and in double the time. (Okay, I know that's being pretty reductive about both films, but that's my immediate reaction now the credits have finished and this is my crappy Letterboxd account so I'll do as I please.) While technically outstanding, I can't say I especially rate A Brighter Summer Day . Many seem to praise its sprawling, “novelistic” style but I'm in the minority here saying that works against the film, which would be much better served with a sharper focus. Praise the 100+ speaking parts all you want, but three hours in my partner and I were still saying things like, “Which boy is Airplane again?” There are too many little distractions taking away from what's really important. On that note, the card at the start telling you that youths are starting gangs because of a lack of identity and security does a lot of heavy lifting, because Yang doesn't show any of that. I know the director has more filmmaking talent in a speck of his dandruff than I do in my entire body, but I still think this is a failing of his and the film. (The kids singing songs in English doesn't scream identity crisis for me, sorry. People all around the world enjoy songs not in their native language – you could probably draw a historical line from Italian and Germanic operas all the way to K-pop to demonstrate this point – so this argument doesn't hold much weight for me, sorry.) Lastly, I have issues with both S'ir and Ming that affect my view of the film. It's tough to discuss without spoilers but I was shaking my head at both come the end. I think we're given too little insight into S'ir's interiority to really, let's say, “appreciate” what comes at the film's climax. Perhaps Yang wants us to be shocked/frustrated/confused by A Brighter Summer Day's seemingly irrational outcome, but without sufficient context, it lacks impact.

texto: J'avais fait une bête de review mais elle s'est pas enregistrée donc tant pis je vais vous faire un résumé. En gros le film est beau et sous-tend un contexte social et historique intéressant (l'immigration de milliers de Chinois à Taïwan après l'élection du parti communiste dans les années 60), mais tout est parasité par les personnages qui sont des gamins et qui agissent donc comme des gamins. On a beau retrouver ce côté "épopée familiale" des films d'Edward Yang qui est très sympa, avec toujours plusieurs personnages et petites sous-histoires qu'on suit en parallèle, je n'ai pas réussi à rentrer dedans, et pour un film de 4h c'est plutôt embêtant. texto: Wanted to connect with this the way I did with Yi Yi , but alas. Regardless, it’s a thorough restoration from Criterion that does justice to Yang’s vision. The guy was a creative visionary, no doubt about it. This epic pushes 4 hours with a focus on the lives of the Taiwanese children of Chinese expats/refugees fleeing mainland China after the Civil War. Though one could be mistaken in thinking the gang ‘turf war’ is only nominally a “war”, Yang disabuses us of that notion as he captures dramatic scenes of street violence, targeted hits on youth leaders and juvenile delinquency of all forms. The kids are abused and neglected at home, and they re-assert familiar power structures in the *playgrounds (*the tennis court, the music hall, the restaurant). Yang’s only music comes in diegetic form via ‘50s Western rock ‘n roll hits and sappy love ballads from Ricky Nelson to Elvis whom the characters adore. It’s a tapestry of a specific place during a specific moment in time under unique political circumstances, but for me, Yang seems unable to bridge the knowledge gap with the audience enough to make me care, especially given this runs at a punishingly languid pace.

texto: I don't really feel like going along with the delusion that this isn’t just unnecessarily long. Given the brief synopsis, I expected a 4-hour run time to give us a plethora of experiences. Instead, we get repetition. Repetition and repetition. Extraordinarily little character growth and slow, ultimately meaningless expansion on the same few themes. It's well made. You are drawn in by the emotion. If you are looking for more of an experience than a movie, then, yes, this is up in that 4+ star range it seems overstuffed with. The point is the grinding, slow despair and after 4 hours you are one with the characters. I don't think 4 hours were needed to make the ending impactful. Many movies can do the same in less than 2. I'm just not here for that experience and the story itself could be effortless wrapped up in 90-120 minutes. There are multiple storylines that are completely unnecessary in any reasonable interpretation of the story, such as the filmmaking one. I didn't dislike this and the run time didn't elicit any negative reaction, probably because I watched it over quite a few installments. I just think, again, there was so much that is unnecessary. I won't say self-indulgent, because I don't think that's what they were going for, I think it's to draw you in to what the filmmakers and characters lives were like, as I said. An OK, but not enthusiasic rating from me.

texto: This feels like one of those movies that is purposely vague in key ways to allow the audience to imprint onto it, and that kind of film is never going to work for me. At its core, we have a father and daughter on vacation together. There are moments where they bond. There is obvious childhood tragedy for the father, which is probably why he seems to drink a lot, yet he's not one of those abusive drunks, so it's ok? We're never really given much depth beyond that. It's a girl growing up, having a first kiss, hanging with other kids on vacation. It's nice that there isn't any kind of bullying or any other overtly negative elements that usually make up these narratives. It's mostly just moments shared between father and daughter, mostly bonding. At the same time, not much actually happens for the entire runtime. There seems to be implied longing, but again, the narrative is kept vague on purpose so that we can somehow imprint on it. The thing is, I am not watching a movie to do its job for it. If there isn't much story there, I'm not going to fill in the blanks for it. If I want to do that, I will either work on one of my own stories or read a book. Is this supposed to be sad and reflective? I never got to vacation with my father before he died when I was around 8 or 9, I never got these moments with him... and to have it be such a positive experience... this girl is fortunate. All I know is real tragedy related to my father. Did the girl's father die right after this? Or was it years later? We see her as an adult, all reflecting and shit, but as I said, things are left mostly vague, so who knows? At least she has cherished moments with her father. More than a lot of us got. On top of that, I think people confuse realism for good. Yeah, it is shot very realistically, the performances are very natural, yet story wise, there isn't much there, and I really dislike the way this was shot, which is probably one of the main sticking points for me. Often badly framed, or where it often focuses on 'experiencing', rather than what they are experiencing, so for instance, they are playing pool, we see them take the shot, but not any of what's actually happening in the game. Or another instance, they play an arcade game, but we never really see what they are playing. As for the bad framing, at times people are talking and the frame is like whatever. Or like, the scene where there is a TV, a mirror behind it, and the whole scene is either shot from a camcorder feeding to the TV or later, when the camcorder is off, what we barely see in the reflection on the screen or in the fragment of exposed mirror is all we get. It is certainly a choice. Oh, I get it, being so 'artistic' in its reflection on what's happening with the character, but it goes on for too long and it's just badly framed, all of it. Or this repeated cutting to a dance club, flashing lights, to show this reoccurring element of the father dancing... but mostly, it is just hard to see anything. Too much of the film is like this. Extended scenes of someone laying around, or badly framed shots like this that are clearly intended to be artistic, but end up being that in a bad way. I remember reading positive comments about this film and it sounds like it should be a good one, right? I expect a level of crudeness from a documentary, because it is trying to capture something in a moment and bring it all together, but when it's a narrative film that looks mostly like a badly shot documentary, that seems to have less story than many documentaries... what are we even doing here?

texto: Alrighty then. Aftersun... it's nothing much. Sure, it's tender a little psychological but there's not much worth digging into here. It's a solemn, minimal film; very few characters, brief interactions and a hazy, dream-like presentation. The whole thing plays out like a distant memory that, seemed happy once, but as you age, you see the sad undercurrents of it. Neat idea, but the execution was spacey and pretentious. Aftersun follows a recently divorced dad and his young daughter on vacation. He's depressed and doing his best to hide it from her. She is growing up, starting to feel attractions and is making real connections with other humans. As the vacation goes on, the daughter and father begin to relate to each other on a deeper level. That's it. Aftersun is good insofar as you relate to it. Most people my age on this site come from fucked up, divorced, miserable families so they have these decaying memories. They look back and realize when they started to realize the cracks. They remember discovering how flawed and broken their parents were; coming of age in a world of dysfunction. I can't really relate so this movie didn't have as much meaning for ol' D.W. The Rumsfelds have always been intact. For me, it was a plodding, gimmicky bore that should have just been a short film or something. I'll never forget the first time I saw my father cry... but that doesn't make this movie good. The characters were middling; mostly slates for the audience to project their sadness onto. Alot of the editing was stupid too, and only sometimes justified. I did like the cinematography and acting, though, Paul Mescal is promising and I have liked almost all of his theatrical performances thus far. Aftersun didn't hold much value for me. I felt like it wasted alot of time and tried to pull heartstrings. It had good focus and some intentionality but when all was said and done, I just kinda threw my hands up in frustration. Pithy abstraction, faux-cuteness, faint natalism, not for me. Two Mutzies and Odenkirk-grade singing

Often badly framed, or where it often focuses on 'experiencing', rather than what they are experiencing, so for instance, they are playing pool, we see them take the shot, but not any of what's actually happening in the game. Or another instance, they play an arcade game, but we never really see what they are playing. As for the bad framing, at times people are talking and the frame is like whatever. Or like, the scene where there is a TV, a mirror behind it, and the whole scene is either shot from a camcorder feeding to the TV or later, when the camcorder is off, what we barely see in the reflection on the screen or in the fragment of exposed mirror is all we get. It is certainly a choice. Oh, I get it, being so 'artistic' in its reflection on what's happening with the character, but it goes on for too long and it's just badly framed, all of it. Or this repeated cutting to a dance club, flashing lights, to show this reoccurring element of the father dancing... but mostly, it is just hard to see anything. Too much of the film is like this. Extended scenes of someone laying around, or badly framed shots like this that are clearly intended to be artistic, but end up being that in a bad way. I remember reading positive comments about this film and it sounds like it should be a good one, right? I expect a level of crudeness from a documentary, because it is trying to capture something in a moment and bring it all together, but when it's a narrative film that looks mostly like a badly shot documentary, that seems to have less story than many documentaries... what are we even doing here?

texto: I entered this with a fair bit of hype, so when I left rather confused about the hype, well... Yeah. There's a banger of a film here, but it only really became somewhat interesting past the halfway mark. Cut out 15-odd minutes of the first or 2nd act, then I think I would rate this movie higher. It's a coming-of-age tale about a father and his 11 year old daughter, on a holiday in turkey. We are given backstory about them as the film goes on, but again, only really after the halfway point. When it became really interesting, and I could tell the movie was wrapping up, I was rather sad as I wanted it to continue in the timeline of these characters, especially the daughter. I can accept the ending of the father as that was really well done, but the daughter? Naaaah, man, keep it going. At that point I was interested in the two leads, interested in the teasers we were shown in flash-forwards, and for sure I picked up on things that happened to Sophie that impacted the future, but again, I wanted more haha. So what did I like? It's really well shot, with a few "one perfect shot" worthy frames. For those who have seen it, two that instantly come to mind are the airport terminal with the father and the tv screenshot in the hotel room where the mirror is somewhat in frame. Plus, the writing of the two leads as mentioned before were great, I really did become interested in them after a bit, but it almost felt too little too late. There are some great character moments here, but besides that, felt like a film with... Not much. TL;DR: A great 85 minute movie here, and I wish it was a bit different in terms of pacing and the timeline of the movie. Seen at the Edinburgh International Film Festival.

texto: J'ai trouvé le film très lent et il manque, selon moi, de dynamisme. Pendant une grande partie du film, j'ai eu du mal à être réellement captivé, la seule scène qui m'a vraiment marqué est la séquence finale, lorsque le père et sa fille dansent ensemble avant la fin de leurs vacances. Les flashbacks qui s'entremêlent à ce moment donnent enfin tout son sens au film et apportent une forte charge émotionnelle. Le film montre avec beaucoup de subtilité comment le père cache sa souffrance pour préserver sa fille. En apparence, il essaie de lui offrir de belles vacances, mais on comprend qu'au fond il est profondément triste et terriblement seul. Il est père célibataire, confronté à des difficultés financières et sans véritable entourage, il porte un mal-être qu'il ne parvient plus à surmonter. La fin révèle également que l'on suivait en réalité les souvenirs de Sophie devenue adulte. Avec le recul, elle comprend enfin les signes qu'elle n'avait pas vus enfant et réalise à quel point son père allait mal avant son décès. Même si je n'ai pas été emballé par le rythme du film, je reconnais que cette conclusion est particulièrement touchante et donne une autre dimension a l’histoire .

texto: J'ai trouvé le film très lent et il manque, selon moi, de dynamisme. Pendant une grande partie du film, j'ai eu du mal à être réellement captivé, la seule scène qui m'a vraiment marqué est la séquence finale, lorsque le père et sa fille dansent ensemble avant la fin de leurs vacances. Les flashbacks qui s'entremêlent à ce moment donnent enfin tout son sens au film et apportent une forte charge émotionnelle. Le film montre avec beaucoup de subtilité comment le père cache sa souffrance pour préserver sa fille. En apparence, il essaie de lui offrir de belles vacances, mais on comprend qu'au fond il est profondément triste et terriblement seul. Il est père célibataire, confronté à des difficultés financières et sans véritable entourage, il porte un mal-être qu'il ne parvient plus à surmonter. La fin révèle également que l'on suivait en réalité les souvenirs de Sophie devenue adulte. Avec le recul, elle comprend enfin les signes qu'elle n'avait pas vus enfant et réalise à quel point son père allait mal avant son décès. Même si je n'ai pas été emballé par le rythme du film, je reconnais que cette conclusion est particulièrement touchante et donne une autre dimension a l’histoire .

texto: This was a movie which i didnt understand and definitely need to rewatch. Incredible acting from Mescal and Corio. Was clearly a movie which leans heavily on the bond between father and daughter and deals with the crippling depression which Mescal's character tries to hide from his daughter, Sophie. From the first sort of 20 minutes, you can tell that this film is showing and not telling , whether it's the very long shots focused on a single subject, or the use of solemn and dark composed music for the film within moments which do not warrant it, the film portrays depression in a much more subconscious way than ive seen other films and series manage. The use of the rave scenes, and lingering shots on what seems like random subjects are something I should analyse on a rewatch, as I am no film buff and therefore have not been able to pick up on the purpose of these scenes and what the intention of the cinematography is very well. The consistently sinister or sombre music being draped over the scenes in this film is representative of how depression consumes every waking minute of a person's life. I believe there was also a theme of a young person being introduced to the world of romance and sexual exploration, with lingering shots of teenagers kissing whilst Sophie was nearby, or that one scene of her overhearing some teenagers talking about a sexual experience. I initially assumed that the sinister and sombre music being used during these scenes was to represent how a young individual's introduction to sexual experiences from others educating said person could represent grooming. However upon research for this film's meaning, I found that this might not be the case? Sex as a theme isnt really a topic discussed online (or at least on reddit) So perhaps for that reason I dont think these scenes are about grooming but rather the coming-of-age experience of discovering romance, love and sex as an additional theme ALONGSIDE the depression Sophie's dad suffers from? If it's not clear, I havent fully understood what this movie is actually about. To really get a better understanding of the film I should rewatch it probably. I liked this film a lot, but oh wow I was very confused.

texto: Boah hat der mich eiskalt erwischt. In „Aftersun“ ging ich mit den Erwartungen rein, ein Drama über die Erforschung von Beziehung zwischen Vater und Tochter zu bekommen. Das gab mir der Film auch, aber auch noch so viel härtere Themen. „Aftersun“ fühlte sich für mich wie eine verlorene Erinnerung an meine Kindheit an. Diese Camcorder aufnahmen sind so dermaßen nostalgisch und schön, dass ich alleine da schon hätte heulen können. Das hier ist so toll gefilmt, die Umgebung und das Setting ist herrlich schön anzusehen und die Cinematographie zum dahinschmelzen. Oftmals erinnerte mich „Aftersun“ von der Erzählung und dem Vibe, an „Nowhere“ von Sofia Coppola welchen ich auch echt gerne mochte. Auch dort geht es ja um recht ähnliches, „Aftersun“ macht das aber nochmal ne ganze Stufe besser, meiner Meinung nach. Irgendwo ist „Aftersun“ ein richtiger feelgood-Film, besonders zu Beginn, die Figuren sind im Urlaub und haben einfach Spaß mit der Zeit die sie zusammen verbringen. Gleichzeitig umgibt den gesamten Film eine so bedrückende Atmosphäre und ein Gefühl von Schwere, Anspannung und Nervosität, was ich anfangs etwas seltsam fand, irgendwann aber so grandios für mich funktionierte. Was ich gehört habe, was vielen nicht gefällt, ist das pacing, weil ja, das ist wirklich sehr langsam. Dafür nutzt der Film diese Zeit und Ruhe um die Erzählung richtig aufzubauen und die Figuren uns nahezubringen, was für mich so gut funktioniert hat, wodurch der Film für mich nie langatmig oder gar langweilig war. Ich habe jetzt so viel Positives zu „Aftersun“ gesagt, ohne mein persönliches Highlight des Films zu nennen, Paul Mescal. Paul Mescal spielt wirklich phänomenal gut. Er und Frankie Corio haben erstmal eine 1a Chemie und sind zusammen so dermaßen süß, dazu spielt Paul Mescal diese Figur mit so einer Tiefe, man spürt bei ihm die ganze Zeit, dass er eine Last in sich trägt, welche im Film nie ausgesprochen wird, aber dennoch durch sein Spiel so deutlich ist, das ist unglaublich. „Aftersun“ hat mich mit seiner Thematik und Erzählung unfassbar gepackt, nicht mehr losgelassen und beinahe zu Tränen gerührt. Nur liebe für diesen Film.

texto: !!!! honestly so speechless. this film has my heart. i can't believe this is charlotte's feature debut. many many thoughts that need to be gathered but oh my goodness i loved this so much. so so much. a searing portrait of father-daughter relationships, adolescence, grief, and parenthood set in the 90s told through the process of remembering a holiday in turkey. it feels like a movie that was made for me—may be too early to say but this might be one of my new all time favorites :') laughed cried reflected the whole shabang 1) what a beautiful debut feature by charlotte wells!!! aghh!!! 2) reminded me of somewhere by sofia coppola from 2010, and the lost daughter too 3) gorgeous GORGEOUS cinematography!! so many frames that i'd love to take and just hang on the wall as artwork. gregory oke has such a great great eye 4) the use of mirrors and surface reflections is striking. reminded me of ozu & kogonada—there's one scene where the camera just stays on the reflection of sophie & callum on the TV as they talk about his past and god it was so good 5) the fact that paul mescal is still very much at the beginning of his career and has two films at cannes right now is kinda insane. he was magnificent <3 6) frankie corio is a revelation 🫶🏼 not shutting up about this movie for the rest of the year! the aftersun publicity campaign starts NOW @ espace miramar, 10.15 PM

exemplo: Várias reviews criticam o fato de o filme ser excessivamente longo, com cenas e diálogos que se estendem demais, tornando a experiência arrastada e difícil de manter o interesse.
texto: c’est un film très lent, avec une atmosphère étrange et de très très très très longs dialogues. c’est un infini procès, avec une embrouille interminable, qui révèle une ambiance très sombre et des personnages tous plus bizarres les uns que les autres. on comprend pas tout et c’est très compliqué d’accrocher. certains plans sont filmées de façon original, et les scènes sont vraiment longues. c’est un film chargé en émotion, avec beaucoup de secrets enfouies. au bout d’un moment ça devient vraiment interminable, des faits surgissent, des hypothèses sont conjecturées, mais c’est jamais explicitement concret. bon ok la façon dont c’est réalisé est très intéressante. par contre, j’ai carrément détesté la fin, pcq tout le long on s’attend à une réponse concrète mais le but du film c’est justement de ne donner aucune réponse, du coup c’est super frustrant. toute l’histoire on peut l’interpréter seulement par des « peut être » et jamais par de véritables faits. chacun des personnages sont intéressants, avec des points de vus différents et des façons de subir la situation différentes, mais le spectateur est à la place des jurés, donc c’est très compliqué de savoir démêlé le vrai du faux. le film rappelle que le verdict ne coïncide pas forcément avec la vérité, et les hypothèses de la potentielle vérité restent plausible. cependant le lien avec le titre du film est très pertinent, en montrant la chute de chacun des personnages de façon disséquées. bon, en toute honnêteté je n’ai pas aimé. le fond du film est émouvant et bien recherché. MAIS, c’est lent + dialogues interminables + bcp de choses abstraites et surtout surtout surtout le film répond à rien, ça te laisse sur ta fin, c’est à toi d’interpréter et de trouver la vérité, la fin est ouverte et ne répond à aucune questions que tu te poses durant tout le film. c’est frustrant et c’est carrément ce que je n’aime pas.

Best Criterion purchase I made since Memories of Murder . ________________________________________________________ Anatomy of a Fall enticed me from the premise alone. A woman is blamed for her husband’s death and the only witness is her blind son. That in it of itself is enough to get my attention. The film is an amazing courtroom drama. It’s similar to A Few Good Men in that every single court sequence is riveting, filled with incredible dialogue and tense confrontations. The movie does a great job creating suspense and tension. I genuinely did not know how it was all gonna play out. What makes this movie stand out though is at its heart, it’s a family drama. It’s about a marriage on the brink of collapse, and how the couple’s issues are impacting their loved ones. It tackles very real topics like infidelity, sexuality, childhood, abuse, depression, and grief. I found myself caring about these characters and the struggles they endured throughout the movie’s runtime. Everything about this movie felt real. Never once did I feel like I was watching a movie. Anatomy of a Fall felt more like someone hid a camera inside someone’s house rather than actors reciting lines from a script (a very well written script I might add) in front of a camera. The authenticity of this film is thanks equally to the screen writer(s) and the actors. Sandra Hüller in particular is downright incredible. The realism of this movie is a bit of a blessing and a curse. I love that the director allowed certain scenes to “breathe.” It created a bunch of heartfelt moments and it gives the viewer the chance to sit with these characters and empathize with them. That being said, I felt like some scenes dragged on for a little too long, and it ruined the pacing in some parts. But once again, maybe on second watch, I’ll feel differently. Bottom line, I love Anatomy of a Fall . I can’t wait to watch it again. In fact I kinda have to watch it again. I watched it while my wife was at book club. When she returned and realized I was watching this movie, she was like “OMG I wanted to watch that too!” Sorry babe. 😜

texto: Palme d’or 2023 et couronné de nombreuses récompenses, Anatomie d’une chute de Justine Triet mérite largement sa réputation. Derrière son apparence de film judiciaire se cache avant tout une dissection fascinante d’un couple en crise, où chaque détail du quotidien prend une importance capitale. Le suspense autour de ce whodunit atypique fonctionne parfaitement, mais le véritable sujet est ailleurs : les ressentis, les incompréhensions et les visions opposées que deux personnes peuvent avoir d’une même histoire. Sandra Hüller livre une prestation remarquable, parvenant à transmettre une multitude d’émotions d’un simple regard. Une réalisation subtile qui nous plonge au plus près des émotions des personnages. Un très bon film.

texto: From the jump this movie’s sound design and framing are next level. Just truly stunning work. As is befitting the French. They don’t do much super well but, boy, can they make movies. There’s something inherently cinematic about the French language. It lends itself to the dramatic. This movie has one of the best openings I have ever seen. Ratcheting up the tension immediately. In particular, a lingering shot on the guide dog of the half blind kid is astounding. The performances in this movie are all fantastic. Funny though, the DOG is the best actor in the movie! You love to see it. The drama brought on by the incompetence (at best) or clear corruption and railroading (at worst) of the French police is infuriating. Especially when you learn that this was inspired by a real case that the Italian police fumbled hard as hell. I love courtroom/crime dramas and this movie is a masterclass in the genre. Highly recommend.

texto: I love movies like this, especially the legal aspect. It’s even better when a film manages to make it feel tense and gripping. The various camera angles and shots were well executed. The plot was greatly enhanced by the atmosphere, the music, and—above all—the characters. I found the acting to be very strong; the lawyer, the mother, the son, and especially the dog all mastered their roles brilliantly. The dog deserves an award! At times during the movie, I genuinely thought the boy was blind in real life (i.e., outside the context of the film). A very convincing performance. As mentioned, the courtroom scenes were a highlight for me, and I found the ending very powerful, too. It evoked a feeling similar to the movie *The Hunt*; the viewing experience felt stark and devoid of the usual clichés. In my opinion, the ending made the most of the situation—even if that statement sounds ironic. Fortunately, the instrumental version of 50 Cent’s "P.I.M.P." was used instead of "Jolene," which had originally been planned; "P.I.M.P." fit the content perfectly.

texto: Classic? I don’t get it! I hadn’t seen this old ‘classic’ film and was looking forward to watching it. However I was left feeling disappointed. As much as I watched ready to be impressed by the storyline or the acting performances, neither really stood the test of time for me. The story line was ok, but rather straightforward, and lacked the nuance or surprise I guess I’ve come to expect from a film like this. The acting felt just a little over exaggerated, each role neither felt a good reflection on the likely behaviour of people in that position, or had the depth of performance where the actor appears to have invested real emotional energy in the task. They were performances, more what I’d expect of the stage. Of course context is everything, and the context of watching this film back in the 50’s will likely of presented to me a very different and more enjoyable proposition. Today though this film won’t live long in the memory and provides little I can recommend to others, as much as I admire James Stewart.

texto: At its best, Anatomy of a Murder is a compelling courtroom drama that showcases the flawless ability of James Stewart and touches on some rather radical takes on understanding why rape culture is so often dismissed and ignored in the court of law. However, the film gets so deep in the repetitive proceedings of the court that it stretches to an absurd 160-minute runtime. Things grow SLOW, and the energy seen in films like 12 Angry Men and The Caine Mutiny Court-Martial fades more and more as the runtime drags. There is the occasional shocking reveal or particularly venomous twist of facts, but for the most part this feels like it is lacking a needed intensity for choosing a scope of this size.

texto: It's a strange film... ​At first glance, the filmmakers seem to think that the heart of the matter lies in whether the wife of the murderer has been violated or not—except they don't. Justifiably so, as they themselves declare in the movie, since that would still not make the murder permissible. Then they swerve to an after-the-fact plea of temporary insanity on the thinnest of evidence. ​The attorney (Stewart) raises smokescreen after smokescreen regarding the possible rape and the murder victim's character, offering very little to substantiate their central defense claim. This, too, his very character admits. I understand exactly what the film is doing here: it is a deliberate critique of the US legal system and juries, exposing the courtroom as a cynical game where truth takes a backseat to theatrics. ​However, while I get the point, the execution feels far too clinical. Spending nearly three hours meticulously building a courtroom drama only to conclude that the entire system is fundamentally broken—and that the truth doesn't actually matter—almost invalidates the film's own narrative. If the whole process is just an empty sham, watching it play out for that long ultimately becomes uninteresting. Because of this detachment, all the characters remain mere caricatures that we never examine more than skin deep. While the filmmakers likely intended to provoke these exact moral questions, the execution is so dry that it feels like reading a well-argued college essay—intellectually sound, perhaps, but it doesn't make for an engaging film. It's a strange film...

texto: fun watch insofar as a trial lawyer, i find trial fun - and some legitimately good trial strategy in here (aided by the fact that in a movie courtroom you get to wax poetic about your objections in the presence of the jury) but nothing profound; difficult not to compare to witness for the prosecution, which i just also watched and liked a bit more; though ultimately i am glad they both deal with, in some way, the idea that our justice system tolerates, as it should, the non-conviction of people who did bad things i genuinely may use this banger quote in a closing: "Twelve people go off into a room: twelve different minds, twelve different hearts, from twelve different walks of life; twelve sets of eyes, ears, shapes, and sizes. And these twelve people are asked to judge another human being as different from them as they are from each other. And in their judgment, they must become of one mind - unanimous. It's one of the miracles of Man's disorganized soul that they can do it, and in most instances, do it right well. God bless juries."

Actually feels like you’re in the courtroom just watching a trial, albeit with some outbursts that feel like they wouldn't fly in real life. With this movie being so morally gray, I found it hard to find someone to root for. I believe that’s the point, but it’s a confusing feeling and not one I enjoyed here. I also did not enjoy the ending. Talk about anticlimactic. They adjourn for the day and then they come back and read the verdict and that’s it, movie over. There was no “silver-bullet” moment in which I was convinced that jury was going to vote one way or the other. So I was still ultimately unconvinced and I personally find it hard to believe the jury was convinced as well. Definitely knocked this movie down a peg for me. While a bit slow, I found the case and performances compelling. The jazz score was nice as well, when you could actually hear it. The court scenes had no score at all. Envelope-pushing and edgy for the time, but I don’t understand the adoration for this movie.

texto: At its best, Anatomy of a Murder is a compelling courtroom drama that showcases the flawless ability of James Stewart and touches on some rather radical takes on understanding why rape culture is so often dismissed and ignored in the court of law. However, the film gets so deep in the repetitive proceedings of the court that it stretches to an absurd 160-minute runtime. Things grow SLOW, and the energy seen in films like 12 Angry Men and The Caine Mutiny Court-Martial fades more and more as the runtime drags. There is the occasional shocking reveal or particularly venomous twist of facts, but for the most part this feels like it is lacking a needed intensity for choosing a scope of this size.

texto: Enjoyable and impressively authentic-feeling courtroom drama, though at nearly three hours it did feel a little long. What I liked most was how procedural it is: you really get a sense of how a defense attorney constructs a case rather than simply uncovering “the truth.” The film never cuts away to show us what actually happened, so we are left with the same uncertainty as the lawyers and jury, weighing testimony, credibility and competing versions of events. That ambiguity is one of the film’s real strengths: the point is not that we eventually discover the truth, but that a legal judgment still has to be reached without anyone (except the accuseds) ever being completely sure of it. Some of the social attitudes are fascinatingly dated, particularly the way Lee Remick’s appearance and sexuality become part of the case. There are also some oddly broad comic touches—the dog, in particular—that felt distracting, and I could have done with less of Stewart’s fishing, law-practice troubles and the subplot involving his alcoholic colleague. The Duke Ellington score is fantastic. Jazz seems like an unlikely choice for a courtroom drama, but it gives the film a distinctive energy and is almost worth the watch by itself. A little bloated and occasionally eccentric, but intelligent, entertaining and unusually convincing.

texto: La película judicial por excelencia; casi tres horas de duración que no se sienten en ningún momento, donde el guion y las actuaciones lo son todo, cómo se nos va revelando cada cosa para luego usarla en el caso y aun así sorprendernos como a los del jurado, una maestría que pocas veces hemos visto en este género. Quizás no tiene las revelaciones más impactantes de la historia, pero sí uno de los mejores ritmos y guiones en la historia del cine. James Stewart la rompe con, posiblemente, la mejor actuación que le haya visto. Tiene un ritmo fabuloso que se divide claramente en dos: una primera parte recolectando los datos para el caso y conociendo a los personajes, y la segunda con todo el juicio, donde todos los datos y revelaciones que vimos se presentan en la corte. Lo mejor de todo es que logra sorprendernos a pesar de que ya sabemos todo lo que pasó en el asesinato. ¿Y saben qué es lo mejor de todo? Su final tan poético, que critica la basura del sistema judicial. Realmente es uno de esos clásicos del cine que envejecieron como el vino. Como casi todos los clásicos (en mi opinión), ha habido películas del mismo género que han sabido llevar de mejor manera el género en el futuro. Aun así, no podemos olvidar de dónde salieron y sus orígenes. Claramente, Anatomy of a Murder es una de las pioneras. Tremendo clásico del cine que tienen que ver mínimo una vez en la vida, sí o sí.

texto: I think this is one of the very best courtroom dramas ever put to screen. It is a complete dissection of the legal system, the people involved, the external factors, and a balance between legality and morality. A lot of films of the same genre rely on the decision of guilt or innocence to drive the narrative, but this movie is completely different. There is so much more to a case than guilt or innocence, and this movie explores it all. Court is normally presented as this place of structure, but in reality it is a game of push and pull to sway the jury to your side. It is all about theatrics to a point where the facts almost begin to take a backseat. Not only is the legal system in question, but the act itself is, as well. A case that seems so open-and-shut is never so simple. On a different note, Jimmy Stewart is Jimmy Stewart. It was an absolute pleasure to watch him play tug-of-war with George C. Scott and even Joseph Welch for almost three hours.

texto: Anatomy of a Murder forms quite an intriguing investigative drama. This confidently serves up what is perhaps the most comprehensive onscreen treatment of the judicial process. Frank matter-of-fact discussion of the main subject matter must've been quite the shock back in the "squeaky-clean" times of 1959. The counselors don't beat around the bush here. They talk about sex, rape, and murder... for lack of better terms. It's striking how relevant that particular aspect rings nowadays, especially in regard to how lawyers, officers, and judicial figures speak about women in cases involving them in any capacity. While inspired by an actual case circa 1952, the film feels ahead of its time in laying out the information to the audience. Otto Preminger's patient, level-headed direction allows what could've been melodrama to instead become a true-to-life mystery... and a fascinating mental exercise. James Stewart reliably offers yet another excellent performance. It's clever how this film plays with the trusted authority type we'd expect him to fill, notably when the trial gets heated. The ensemble cast acquits themselves superbly (no pun intended). Lee Remmick treads the line between desperate wife and seductive femme like the palm of her hand. Ben Gazzarra spiritedly lends intensity and grit into his defendant, fueling the stakes in his position. George C. Scott, Orson Bean, and Joseph N. Welch steal their scenes with such vivid presence (loud or quiet). The strength of all their performances on top of an astute script already warrants a physical media purchase. Preminger takes it further by developing an absorbing style that enables the back-and-forth to be so engaging. Charm, warmth, intrigue, and crackling dialogue foster strong interest well before the defense accepts their client. The additional layer of ambiguity kept me guessing even while I was fairly certain of how the proceedings would play out. Moreover, any viewer can read each beat, detail, and revelation differently to walk away with varying conclusions, no matter the ultimate ruling. Makes for a haunting ending that leaves a silver lining of sorts. Moody cinematography bathes in the noir aesthetic and adds considerable flair to it. Fantastic framing throughout! Some shots move in the right way at the right time, whether a gradual glide or a frantic snap. Duke Ellington delivers a ritzy jazz score that's also willing to be melancholy at points. Really dug the main menu music on the Criterion DVD, which also rules when heard in its proper context. I would advise against watching this late at night, lest you become sleepy and miss a crucial moment. Its slower burn through 2 hours and 40 minutes does accurately convey how it feels to observe a trial. Your mileage will vary there. One side character's odd detour and a couple repetitive motions stall the momentum a tad. Though I can say overall the film's a far more efficient use of time than actual jury duty. After sorting through and analyzing its intricately stitched pieces, I can attest that Anatomy of a Murder stands as a classic. Viewing several of its genre peers earlier this year (from Philadelphia to Coyote vs. Acme ) may have diluted the impact for me. Nonetheless, it's an excellent picture bearing esteemed influence.

texto: Enjoyable and impressively authentic-feeling courtroom drama, though at nearly three hours it did feel a little long. What I liked most was how procedural it is: you really get a sense of how a defense attorney constructs a case rather than simply uncovering “the truth.” The film never cuts away to show us what actually happened, so we are left with the same uncertainty as the lawyers and jury, weighing testimony, credibility and competing versions of events. That ambiguity is one of the film’s real strengths: the point is not that we eventually discover the truth, but that a legal judgment still has to be reached without anyone (except the accuseds) ever being completely sure of it. Some of the social attitudes are fascinatingly dated, particularly the way Lee Remick’s appearance and sexuality become part of the case. There are also some oddly broad comic touches—the dog, in particular—that felt distracting, and I could have done with less of Stewart’s fishing, law-practice troubles and the subplot involving his alcoholic colleague. The Duke Ellington score is fantastic. Jazz seems like an unlikely choice for a courtroom drama, but it gives the film a distinctive energy and is almost worth the watch by itself. A little bloated and occasionally eccentric, but intelligent, entertaining and unusually convincing.

texto: This movie was not exactly what I was expecting. I feel as though it could more accurately have been called Anatomy of a Rape with its surprisingly prominent repeated references to panties and an explanation of spermatogenesis , which I was definitely not expecting in a movie from 1959. Right up to the end I was anticipating there to be a twist, and of course there was, although I have to say that it was something of a letdown. Nevertheless there were some wonderful lines of dialogue in the snappy exchanges between the lawyers and the judge and some unexpectedly humourous moments. However it is a really long movie which undoubtedly drags a bit on occasions with its very lengthy courtroom scenes. There was undeniably inappropriate sexual tension between Jimmy Stewart as the defendant's lawyer and Lee Remick as the defendant's wife, as she confidently stated in a matter-of-fact way, that, of course he was gazing upon her lustfully, as all men do. Also some typically sixties sexism in Pauly’s interactions with his assistant Maida, who for me was still the best character. In the end I managed to forgive any such shortcomings as incidental, putting them down to being merely a consequence of the era, and enjoyed the complexities of the movie immensely. Sue me. Oh yes, bonus points for Muffy the dog.

texto: I was pleasantly surprised by this one, I don't know that I'd agree if someone told me it's almost three hours long in a couple of days from now, it's such a captivating film that it literally feels like it goes by in absolutely no time. I went into it expecting an unforeseen plot twist a la Witness for the Prosecution, and maybe that's exactly why I was pleasantly surprised. The film takes its story seriously and immerses you into a pool of moral quandaries that are hard to get out of precisely because of one's lack of knowledge of the truth. At the same time as it shows you the many societal obstacles there are to the believability and the respectability of women's testimonies of abuse due to social prejudice even within what is supposed to be a serious legal process, it at the same time makes you question not necessarily that the story behind it might be a complete fabrication, but that the motivations for positioning such abuse at the center of it all might actually end up contributing to the further societal incarceration of the woman at the center of it all. I can definitely see why Anatomy of a Fall takes after the name of this one, and, even if I consider that one to be an even more sofisticated version of the educated paranoia that takes over the viewer purely via the uncertainty of judicial proceedings, this is still a very respectable film, one of those everyone should see at least once in their lifetime if that makes any sense.

texto: القصة القصيرة «حرق الحظيرة» لهاروكي موراكامي كانت بالنسبة لي أفضل بكتير، وكافية بذاتها بما فيها من رمزية وأفكار جميلة: الشر يظهر بلا سبب واضح. والمخيف يبدو طبيعي جدًا. لا يظهر كشيطان بقرون بل يرتدي زي أنيق. والخطر موجود لكن لا يمكن إثباته. ونخلق أوهام.. ونصدقها.. ونعيش عليها. الحظائر أو البيوت البلاستيك تمثل الأشياء المهملة والبشر غير المرئيين اجتماعيًا، وأقربهم الفتاة نفسها.. ضائعة في الحياة وذاتها، تبحث عن أي يد تتعلق بها فلا تجد أحدا حقيقي، ولكن هي تجعله حقيقي ومناسب بتصديق الوهم في عقلها، ولانه كان جذاب ف صدقت. الرجل الثري يجسد فراغ الطبقة المترفة، والبطل عجز الإنسان العادي أمام شر لا يستطيع فهمه أو مواجهته. أما الفيلم فبالنسبة لي مط القصة أكثر من اللازم، وطال بلا داع وممل، والنهاية أغلقت باب التساؤلات الذي كانت القصة أجمل بتركه مفتوح.

texto: Beautifully directed and shot, with an incredible atmosphere and some truly gorgeous cinematography. The performances are also great, especially considering how subtle the film is. But honestly, I found the story frustratingly slow. For most of the runtime, I kept waiting for something to actually happen, and by the end I was left thinking: “Is that it?” I appreciate the ambiguity and everything the film is trying to say, but emotionally and narratively, it just didn’t do enough for me. Great filmmaking, but not a film I loved.

texto: I really wasn’t the biggest fan of this movie even though I really wanted to be. Nothing really ever clicked for me to like this, I really disliked how open ended they kept it. I’m usually a fan of keeping something ambiguous but just feel like their attempt at it fell flat. The first 30 minutes were basically pointless, just showed a sex scene and two scenes just watching the main character jerk off. It really doesn’t start to get going until Steven Yeuns character pulls up. Even when he comes in it still feels extremely slow and avoids really digging deep into any big ideas. Really didn’t feel any suspense towards the end when it tries to turn into a thriller type of vibe. The main charter was so unlikeable, at his core he was a total loser who takes all his built up anger out on Ben in a pretty messy climax to the movie. I did really enjoy the cinematography and Steven Yeuns performance. Besides that I was not a fan, it also really didn’t help that the subtitles were about 2 seconds ahead of the dialogue so it was very hard to follow a lot of the dialogue. May need a rewatch because of this.

texto: Very subtle and creeping directorial style, really it's almost unnoticeable with how naturally the story flows from start to finish. You really have to pay close attention to fully appreciate its brilliance. The film's use of natural light was awesome, the cinematography had this way of making even the most unremarkable locations aesthetically pleasing. I love how the narrative took its time establishing and really building up the characters, as it progresses, further depth is added to each of them, which kept the mystery really gripping and unpredictable. I thought the film chose the best and most satisfying path to conclude on, answering the question regarding her whereabouts would've been lame, especially after all that amazing buildup. I usually dislike these type of ending because they often feel more like the director just wasn't able to provide a satisfactory answer to the question they posed, but in this film's case it's different, it didn't feel like a cop out, but really more of a conscious choice, one that encourages a further and more in depth rewatch.

texto: Very subtle and creeping directorial style, really it's almost unnoticeable with how naturally the story flows from start to finish. You really have to pay close attention to fully appreciate its brilliance. The film's use of natural light was awesome, the cinematography had this way of making even the most unremarkable locations aesthetically pleasing. I love how the narrative took its time establishing and really building up the characters, as it progresses, further depth is added to each of them, which kept the mystery really gripping and unpredictable. I thought the film chose the best and most satisfying path to conclude on, answering the question regarding her whereabouts would've been lame, especially after all that amazing buildup. I usually dislike these type of ending because they often feel more like the director just wasn't able to provide a satisfactory answer to the question they posed, but in this film's case it's different, it didn't feel like a cop out, but really more of a conscious choice, one that encourages a further and more in depth rewatch.

texto: Assisti com meu marido, e juntos representamos a média das reviews aqui: eu amei, ele odiou 😜 Para mim, Burning e seu roteiro extraordinário nos dá tempo de acompanhar e conhecer Jong-Su e sua solitude, o reencontro que cresce em uma paixão e exposição aos extremos da desigualdade social. Jong-Su e Hae-Me, pra mim, ambos tem a "grande fome", por a expõem ao mundo em suas maneiras distintas. Apesar disso, ambos partem do mesmo lugar, inclusive em termos de casta, de classe, de lugar naquela sociedade - ambos no oposto de Ben. "Esquecer que algo não existe", memória e nem sabermos se de fato Boil existe, ou as aulas de pantomima, ou o poço, essa ambiguidade que se extende ao hobby de 'queimar estufas', todo esse efeito "gato de schroedinger" me fizeram perceber que até aquele final, nós somos Jong-Su. Só temos essas ambiguidades, os misterios, o obvio que Ben a matou e que isso tudo é uma grande metáfora para cremação... ou tráfico humano?? Afinal, ele nunca diz o que faz da vida. Não sabemos. Mas que Jong-Su queimou, queimou. Um dos usos de ambiguidade, de fotografia mais lindos que ja vi

texto: What strikes me the most about Lee Chang-dong's Burning is that throughout its entire 2 hour and 28 minute runtime, nothing happens. This is partly untrue, Burning's second half concedes to some minute thriller conventions but never fully yields to being a standard, by the book thriller. Instead, much of it is this masculine ego war between two men. Two men from completely opposite social classes. The first of these two men is Jong-su, an aspiring writer unable to find employment in Korea's rigidly competitive job market. He's curious and always questions the world around him, and he's very well aware of his class standing. He's aware of the material conditions around him, and he seems to have some sort of knowledge on the issues of capitalism and imperialism (even if this is never outwardly revealed). And standing opposing to him is Ben. Ben is this mysterious figure who stands blissfully ignorant to the world around him. He gets to do so because he's one of the upper elites. And when the inciting incident about halfway into the film occurs, the film becomes a silent battle between the two, attempting to dominate the other, Jong-su channeling his jealousy of Ben's lifestyle while Ben attempts to use his status to elevate himself over Jong-su. However, it is almost impossible to talk about Burning without mentioning the most important character of the film (in my opinion at least), is Hae-Mi. If Jong-su represented the alienation and repressed anger of the lower class Koreans, Hae-Mi serves as an allegory for how women are stripped of their agency under capitalism and its brutal class system. Early on the film, Hae-Mi is introduced to the audience as an old friend of Jong-su, and they go for a dinner together. Here she explains two metaphors, "Little Hunger" and "Great Hunger". "Little Hunger", she says, is the immediate desires of humanity, to fulfill their literal hunger and to survive. However, she then elaborates that the "Great Hunger" is humanity's hunger for meaning in life, some objective truth to the absurdity we live in. Her story is one of the most important parts of the film, yet it is completely depicted through the eyes of Jong-su. It is established that he is completely obsessed over her, yet the film never highlights how much of that love is truly real, or is some infatuation. Through his gaze, she is completely stripped of her agency, mirroring the film's commentary on patriarchy in a Korean society as well. When Hae-Mi dances in the sunset, high on weed and naked from the top, the film drifts into its most hypnotic and stunning. The visuals are truly incredible during this scene, and I was utterly captivated throughout her ritualistic performance. Jong-sus jealousy of her and Ben turned into misogyny and here, as he angrily refers to her as a "whore", the audience begins to see the pent up anger spew out with uncomfortable misogyny, which boils into the final act of the film. Yet, as the end arrived, the film refused to provide any answers. Which is why the ending had more than a few people feel it was futile. There's no final answer, no twist to shock the viewers. Nothing. With this, Lee Chang-dong even questions the genre's conventions of objective finalities, that the final act of violence has any meaning in solving the mystery of the film. The film asserts the mystery isn't the point, the pointlessness IS the point. Whether an objective truth can ever be found is unlikely, all humanity can live on are interpretations of narratives and ideas we build in our heads.

texto: Solid neo-noir that I tried to connect with. I seemed well-equipped to enjoy Burning. I held an affinity for love triangles and mystery, I liked fire motifs, and I also had ample personal lore for the film to mean something to me. However, its impact never hit. Perhaps Burning would’ve had a stronger impact if it focused on Jong-Su and Haemi’s intertwined fates. Facing the same odds in life, the only differing factor was their sex. Unfortunately the film seemed preoccupied with making Haemi’s struggle picturesque and easy to consume. Her hopelessness was unconvincing, not in a way that strengthened the mystery either. She just seemed a little too objectified for my liking. Respectfully, I don’t think weed makes you do all that. When the film was recommended to me, much of the emphasis was on Steven Yeun’s acting. The praise felt contrived; his acting was stellar but the character wasn’t utilised to its full potential for it to be memorable. Burning introduces itself as a Murakami adaptation, but I learnt later that Murakami’s short story was adapted from Faulkner’s work. There’s a rich intertextuality that is missing from my assessment of the film, and I’m inclined to fill that gap. Doing so might distinguish it from Blow-Up, The Long Goodbye, Under the Silver Lake, quietly haunting films about intrigue and ennui. Complaints and praises alike, Burning spurred many subsequent discussions. When asked if the film was more of a window of discovery or a mirror for introspection, I jokingly likened it to a well. Perhaps that’s true. Refreshment and nourishment were there, but somewhat out of reach, drying up even 🫣 And the field of vision was narrow, but one could catch sparse insights if you stared long enough.

texto: Idk. Sometime around Inglorious Basterds Tarantino crawled way too far up his own ass and he started trying to elevate his style of airy pulpy pastiche by grounding it in these very historicized settings and trying his hand at some revisionism. I think this largely exposes his strengths and weaknesses as a filmmaker, his strengths being that he knows a lot about movies and is inspired by some of the best filmmakers and films of new Hollywood and his earnest efforts of carrying that tradition on is touching, and his weaknesses being that he’s stupid and has very close minded views of everything and has very reactionary sensibilities. Hard to muster much of my thoughts on Django specifically because all of QTs films follow the same beats and thus have the same structural flaws. But I’ll say that while there’s a lot of righteous violence and catharsis for Django against white slavers, there is equal parts gratuitous violence against black slaves used for little more than exploitative window dressing.

texto: i feel like i’m crazy. this movie is so indulgent, so exploitative, and so gratuitous. i think it’s a necessary story. pre-civil war and the arc of a freed black man as a western makes a lot of sense. tarantino was not the man who should have done it, and the tone of this film is insulting. this setting is not the one for dark comedy. people can do what they want, they can enjoy what they want, but i find this film completely irresponsible. not only do we still have a white savior in mr. schultz, but we spend the most time with a black slave owner as an antagonist. the film plays white antagonism as a joke or comedic relief, while samuel l. jackson is played like a real villain. i suppose there is an argument to be made for dicaprio, but mr. shultz defeats him, not even our black protagonist. the messaging is all over the place. it fails to comment on the lack of true power black people could ever have in this time period by being dishonest about the positions of power they are put in in this film. the other enslaved people we see, other than the people being whipped or eaten by dogs, seem peaceful and willing. i think it paints an inaccurate picture. not to mention, what good does it do to show so much violence against enslaved people? we can use it sparingly, that’s okay, but general audiences won’t understand the gravity of the violence against enslaved people when they see it within a comedy like this. “American Slavery Was Not A Sergio Leone Spaghetti Western. It Was A Holocaust. My Ancestors Are Slaves. Stolen From Africa. I Will Honor Them.“ - spike lee maybe i’m missing something. please enlighten me. but i found this to be egregious.

texto: As a black female adult, I’ve come to realization that I hated  this movie solely because how Quentin Tarantino portrays the  whole concept of a enslaved man became free based on a white bounty hunter and helped him kill different slave masters. The whole movie didn’t sit right with me. To be honest, as a southern black woman herself it made my blood boiled. I had to cut the movie off halfway when I saw the scene of two black man fighting to the death for their slave master as a betting deal and entertainment. I understand he was trying to get the concept of how it was back than but I felt that it was unnecessary that every sentence or dialogue was n***a this and n***a that. An a white man directing a ‘black slave movie’ showing the different trademarks of how black people was treated, punished, and abused doesn’t sit right. Basically showing it from a white point of view than black point of view. There’s a difference. I didn’t feel educated not one bit to how my ancestors were treated back than. I used to love this as kid but as I became older I realized that this movie is disrespectful towards black people and I stand by that.

texto: [22/100] Whenever I would have my representational quibbles over this, over whether the prolonged episodes of black suffering told through this exploitation lens for two hours is worth it for the cathartic bloodbath, over whether Tarantino's quippy, witty dialogue (extraordinarily poor here - rarely a memorable exchange in this) fits immediately following, for example, the mauling of a slave by a dog, whether or not it is a lack of writerly and directorial quality in this one that makes it work less than Basterds or if that film was set in and around the concentration camps it may have had an equally repellent and vulgar effect... Whenever I would think all these things, I would remember this video and I would feel even more unsure about whether this guy is really the one to be making this film. Then, he shows up in a terribly plotted distraction near the end doing an appalling Australian accent and it really pushed the question of whether someone who thinks that was a good idea could actually know what he's doing with all these weighty images. I feel comfortable answering that with a blunt 'no' by the end. His worst film by a long shot.

texto: I was about to wonder aloud if I should even comment on not loving this movie given that I'm white, but then I remembered that the dude who made this is, in fact, White Man Quentin Tarantino. Violence against the violent feels good... kinda? Until the whole thing becomes torturous. Was the lead-up violence against slaves only there to make us feel better about the end violence? If so, I am only left with the reality in which that violence was real, but no Django ever came for vengeance in real life. And I get that it's a movie, where anything's possible — but I also can't help the way a movie makes me feel. And this one made me feel gross that there's such a wide audience for this kind of story. I've yet to reach a conclusion. That being said, stars go to the absolutely incredible acting, the soundtrack, some incredible camerawork, and those few moments when I did genuinely feel some relief at (albeit fake) sweet sweet justice.

texto: I think this is just not for me, even on a rewatch I think while there are undeniably great aspects to this film its just so messy as a whole I struggle to get behind anything it puts down. The performances here are probably the biggest detractor, aside from Walz they lack any sort of finesse or styling they are just these over-acted messes I think Leo is the biggest casuality here, Candy at his core feels like he could be a great character but because of Dicaprio's one note performance his character misses any nuance or any quality that would make it stick in my mind for any amount of time. Jamie Foxx feels similarly shallow offering nothing but an attempt at a commanding presence that never feels all that intimidating or striking, and SLJ just kind of flails around. I think because I'm such a huge western fan this one would've have been really special to make it in for me but Tarantino's hodge podge just feels unbalanced insensitive and unfunny. It feels more like a parody of the genre without any understanding what makes the tropes of the genre interesting. Focusing more on reference value and showing the viewer that it is in fact a western than creating something more a cheap roller-coaster ride that certainly has some highs but also makes me reach for the paper bag more than once. The way the film tries to make any sort of a message is baffling to me. Its as if Tarantino got out a balancing scale and was like if I put in loads of goofy and comedic elements but mix it in with loads of edgy, "cool" and violent moments it'll somehow balance out, but to me it just feels disjointed. The film tries to balance the racism it explores with no accountability, there is no justice for D'artagnan just a fuckload of n-slurs. And while the oppressors are brought to justice by the end the way its just handled with zero weight or magnitude makes it all feel worthless by the end. That being said I believe the film really has some fantastic scenes in isolation, the scene where Django shoots his first bounty with Schulz or the one where they're at the dinner table in candy land are still genuinely tense and the opening is really fun, but it's overall tonal dissonance and general feeling of lack of weight make this a dud for me. Not bad just not for me.

texto: Um breve comentário... Revisitando "Django", descobri que possuo uma série de incômodos com esse filme. Não consigo afirmar que é um filme ruim, muito menos que é brilhante. Mas há algo aqui que me incomoda profundamente. E acredito ser a maneira como Tarantino dirige sua violência. Não sua eloquência estética que jorra para todos os lados. Mas as escolhas feitas para a construção do ódio sobre os donos de escravos. Em "Bastardos Inglórios", Tarantino não precisa recorrer aos atos de barbárie da segunda guerra para construir a imagem dos nazistas ou alocar a faixa de "esses são os vilões". Pelo contrário, os atos de barbárie apenas recaem sobre eles (com exceção da introdução de Shosanna), e assim somos levados por toda a história. Mas, aqui? Existe um tratamento com o corpo negro que me causa náuseas. Não só a colocação de Django, em alguns momentos, como um sujeito inocente, infantil, incapaz e que precisa de tutela, mas as introduções de Broomhilda serem sempre pautadas pela transgressão de seu corpo. Sua personagem é uma passageira da agonia frente aos nossos olhos. E aí, o tratamento de ventríloquo que Tarantino dar a seus personagens prejudica a própria substância que os constitui. Broomhilda é apenas uma boneca que está sendo torturada durante todo o filme. Apenas esperando a morte ou a surpresa de seu salvador. É engraçado esse filme vir logo após bastardos. Principalmente pelas decisões tomadas de reconstruir cenas de violência ao corpo negro, quase que com o intuito de fazer com quem o telespectador compre a ideia que o dono de escravos é o "homem mal". Como se ser DONOS DE ESCRAVOS já não fossem suficiente, da mesma maneira que ser nazista. Não falo se a escolha do diretor é certa ou errado, se devia ou não estar ali, mas das sensações que provoca ao telespectador. E sim, acho engraçado que em um filme ele não recorra a barbárie ao povo judeu, mas a corpos negros ele dedica tanto tempo e estilo para isso. Sim, DiCaprio rouba o filme pra si. Sim, a sequência de sua morte e o show de sangue é catártico, como muitos filmes de Tarantino NÃO conseguem ser. Mas até chegarmos a esse ponto, somos levados a uma exploração da violência sobre o corpo negro que me causa náuseas.

texto: listen, it’s not a bad film. as with most tarantino films, i had fun. good visuals, snappy dialogue — though that said, i’m not a fan ot the overuse of the n-word. when creating a film set in this time period dealing with slavery and racism, i know it’s to be expected, but only if you are going to meaningfully delve into those topics. which brings me to my point. sure, the black central character kills a bunch of white racist men, and i will admit that it is satisfying to watch, but past that, there isn’t a whole lot of depth. slavery just feels more like a convenient plot device than an actually relevant theme. django’s whole purpose is to find his wife, but what character is he given outside of that? even the white characters are given more nuance than him. it’s meant to be empowering which it suceeds in some ways but absolutely nothing else

exemplo: As atuações são frequentemente elogiadas como um dos pontos mais fortes, com destaque para Christoph Waltz, Leonardo DiCaprio, Jamie Foxx e Samuel L. Jackson. A química entre os atores principais também é mencionada como um fator que sustenta a história.
texto: Que FILMAÇO! Meu primeiro filme do Tarantino e, cara, é tanta coisa, tantas mensagens que te pegam. Uma hora esse filme te faz sentir raiva, outra hora você ri, outra hora fica eufórico. E, nossa, quantas sensações diferentes em um filme de faroeste. Quanto a uma crítica, não vou tentar me estender muito, mas esse filme facilmente daria uns 20 parágrafos. Bom, o filme é dividido em três arcos muito bem definidos, e eu gostei bastante dessa divisão. É bem explícita a ascensão do Django, a missão para resgatar a Brunilda e, por fim, o clímax. Cada uma dessas partes é muito divertida e cheia de críticas à época da escravidão, ao tratamento dado aos negros, ao racismo e etc. Todas essas críticas são ridiculamente bem escritas e cirúrgicas, justamente por serem secas e te deixarem com raiva daquilo que está sendo mostrado (ou, pelo menos, é isso que deveria acontecer). Ao mesmo tempo, em alguns momentos você consegue rir da situação, seja pelo absurdo, seja pela graça mesmo. As atuações são estupendas. Os três atores principais roubam a cena: Jamie Foxx, Christoph Waltz e Leonardo DiCaprio. Principalmente o DiCaprio. Minha nossa, que vilão bom. Ele é acompanhado por um subvilão, interpretado pelo Samuel L. Jackson, que a todo momento consegue te deixar com raiva. Minha nossa, que raiva desse personagem. O Waltz e o Jamie Foxx também têm uma química que funciona desde o minuto 1 do filme. Os dois são muito bons juntos e conseguem carregar boa parte da história com uma naturalidade absurda. Uma coisa que achei muito interessante foi a evolução do Django. Graças ao roteiro, é perceptível o desenvolvimento dele por meio do letramento e do pensamento individual. É muito satisfatório acompanhar isso e ver como o personagem vai mudando ao longo do filme. A cena da KKK, de longe, é uma das coisas mais engraçadas do filme. É tão idiota que acaba sendo genial, e a cena termina de uma forma espetacular. Pra terminar, só apontar a única (única mesmo) coisa que não gostei: o ritmo do começo. A diferença de ritmo entre o primeiro terço do filme e o momento em que eles conhecem o personagem do DiCaprio fez com que o início demorasse um pouco pra mim. Mas talvez seja só meu cérebro derretido pelo TikTok, enfim, fica aí o comentário. Que filme maravilhoso. Fica a dica.

texto: Django Unchained is an epic 70s western that is visually awesome to see and overly bloody. This is what I expect SO MUCH from Quentin Tarantino. This is the type of movie I’d expect Quentin Tarantino to write and direct this movie with such style. One of the many filmmaking styles that was awesome to see in the movie was the timing on Zoom-in/outs. Every time a major scene happens, the camera usually zoom-in on the actor’s faces. Christoph Waltz, Leonardo DiCaprio, Jamie Foxx, & Samuel L. Jackson were outstanding. Each of the three acts in the movie, I like how the movie tries to separate having the most dialogues in the three acts: bounty hunter Dr. king Schultz in Act 1, the evil and disturbing Calvin Candie in Act 2, & freed slave turned bounty hunter Django Freeman in Act 3. Overall, Django Unchained is a badass movie with great Quentin Tarantino style & Oscar-winning performances from Christoph Waltz & Leonardo DiCaprio. Grade: A+ Score: 9.5/10

texto: “Just because you are a character doesn’t mean you have character.” - Rick Dalton Tarantino really knows how to make a movie about absolutely nothing feel like something. I went into this expecting a typical Tarantino movie and somehow ended up just enjoying the fuck out of watching Rick Dalton and Cliff Booth exist. Leonardo DiCaprio was absolutely hilarious, especially every time Rick started crashing out over his career. Brad Pitt was also fucking perfect as Cliff. Dude just shows up, does whatever the hell he wants, and somehow looks cool doing it. The movie is definitely slow, but I honestly didn’t mind it. I loved the whole Hollywood setting and how it felt like Tarantino was showing his version of what Hollywood used to be. And then that ending… HOLY SHIT. I wasn’t expecting it to go that way at all, and seeing the whole Manson situation get turned into one of the most insane endings was peak Tarantino. The flamethrower scene had me fucking crying. Not my favorite Tarantino movie, but there’s just something about this movie that I really enjoyed. It’s basically three hours of hanging out with two dudes in Hollywood, and somehow I’m completely invested.

texto: Eu fiz algumas pesquisas e descobri que Kubrick era fascinado pela guerra, não por glorificação militar e sim expor a fragilidade e irracionalidade humana. Em Dr. Strangelove Kubrick usou sua brilhante mente para juntar guerra e sexo em uma comédia. Durante o filme acompanhamos homens incompetentes tentando manejar uma guerra como se estivessem brincando num parquinho. Esse é um ponto que me fez rir, porque a crítica de Kubrick é extremamente real. Nas guerras atuais, ainda notamos os "fetiches" de homens no comando de potências globais se divertindo com o desespero alheio. A masculinidade tóxica pode nos levar (ou já está nos levando) a um futuro ridículo. E de novo, a cinematografia é incrível! O enquadramento dos personagens é crucial para uma interpretação mais perspicaz.
