texto: C'est probablement l'un des pires Kubrick selon moi. Le film nous propose une sorte de huis clos politique qui ressemble plus à l'ancêtre de BFM TV qu'à un véritable film. Ça parle, ça reparle, ça rediscute encore et encore pour finalement pas grand-chose. Mais surtout, sans que le film ait réellement l'impression d'avancer. J'ai l'impression d'avoir entendu les mêmes discours pendant 1h30, le même message pendant 1h30, les mêmes phrases pendant 1h30 et surtout les mêmes dialogues répétitifs pendant 1h30. C'est clairement l'emploi du temps de BFM TV ! Les acteurs sont très limités, jusqu'à un point où un seul acteur joue trois personnages différents. C'est peut-être la seule véritable prouesse du film, mais malheureusement, même avec le maquillage, les costumes et les changements de personnage, on le reconnaît immédiatement. Ça devient presque ridicule. Le jeu d'acteur est souvent surjoué et mal dosé. Et surtout, l'humour noir et l'absurdité qu'on m'avait vendus sont quasiment absents. On m'avait vendu un film rempli d'humour noir, d'absurdité et de satire. Au final, j'ai trouvé une ou deux scènes réellement amusantes, mais le reste est beaucoup trop sérieux. Ce n'est même pas vraiment une comédie à mes yeux. L'absurdité apparaît peut-être une ou deux fois, puis disparaît complètement. L'humour noir qu'on m'avait promis s'est littéralement fait cracher dessus avant même d'arriver. Et décidément, un huis clos ne pourra jamais faire mieux que 12 Hommes en colère. La tension est artificielle, les rebondissements sont quasiment inexistants et, pendant 1h30, j'ai surtout eu l'impression de regarder un discours politique interminable. Je ne trouve quasiment rien de cinématographique ou de créatif dans ce film. À part une ou deux scènes rigolotes, il n'y a pas grand-chose qui m'a diverti. Et même la musique me paraît, selon moi, plus créative et plus complète que le film en entier. Elle propose davantage d'idées, d'ambiance et de variété que ce que le film arrive à me proposer pendant 1h30. C'est quand même assez ironique de sortir d'un film en ayant l'impression que sa bande-son est plus intéressante que son propre contenu. Mais il y a quand même quelques passages que j'ai trouvés vraiment réussis. Les séquences autour de la guerre, notamment tout ce qui concerne l'avion et son crash, sont particulièrement bien faites pour l'époque, surtout quand on prend en compte le budget du film. Visuellement, ces passages sont beaucoup plus intéressants et montrent enfin quelque chose de réellement cinématographique. Les indications militaires, le contexte de la guerre et tout ce qui touche à la menace communiste sont également plutôt sympathiques. Ces passages sont malheureusement assez rares, mais lorsqu'ils arrivent, ils m'ont presque permis de ne pas décrocher complètement. C'est peut-être même ce qui m'a empêché de passer mon temps à faire défiler une émission politique comme si je pouvais simplement scroller pour passer à la prochaine émission. Bref, un huis clos ultra simple, peu divertissant et, selon moi, particulièrement vide. Une caricature totale. Et surtout une caricature totalement surcotée...

texto: “film and american society” watch #3 I cannot tell you how excited I was to finally watch this film, both due to its reputation and the admiration I have for Kubrick as a filmmaker, which is why is saddens me greatly to say I didn’t love Dr. Strangelove: or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb . On one hand, I think it’s brilliantly written and effectively captures the simultaneously silly, absurd, and terrifying reality of nuclear warfare and the sociopolitical aspects fully in the hands of man. Naturally, it’s stretched to the extreme given its comically outrageous nature, but in many ways, Dr. Strangelove ’s sharp criticisms  remain relevant today: global annihilation, and consequently the fate of the entirety of humanity, is at the mercy of a bunch of horny, overzealous and incompetent men toying around with hydrogen bombs as if they were play things whilst comparing the sizes of their di-I mean missles. And given it’s a satire, I do find much of Dr. Strangelove to be humorous, and I did get a decent chuckle out of me from time to time. But at the end of the day, I really didn’t find this film to be all the funny. I just feel like it’s a tad bit outdated and, at times, too goofy for its own good. I can certainly see the appeal for others and Kubrick’s audience at the time of it’s release, but there were many instances  where I knew I should have been bursting out laughing, but at most was cracking a smirk. And as I’ve said in previous reviews, films focused solely on politics or historical events typically just don’t do it for me, and I think Dr. Strangelove unfortunately falls into that category for me. The acting is great (Peter Sellers in his triple performance and Sterling Hayden in particular are fantastic) and the story is well-written, but it was unsuccessful in fully sucking me into the chaos and panic of this world. I was sadly a bit bored at times (despite a rather short runtime) and was simultaneously hoping it’d keep going so I could get to a part I loved and wanting it to end. This film, in no way, shape, or form, takes away from my feelings towards Kubrick as an artist. As I’ve said before, I do think it’s cleverly written, well-executed, and impeccably shot film (might I add), with cinematography that once again proves he’s second to none when it comes to knowing the camera and where it should go. But the sociopolitical themes and darkly satirical humor of Dr. Strangelove just didn’t resonate or impact me the way I’d hoped they would. It pains me to say it, but this is my least favorite Kubrick as of now.

texto: The biggest problem, though, is Hans Zimmer, whose score is incredibly loud and unremittingly the dominant sound for more of the movie’s 155 minutes than not. Zimmer’s approach to musical cultural appropriation has been blithe since at least 1994’s The Lion King , while his subsequent rise to Coachella fame has accelerated improbably. Both worlds collide in Dune ’s score, a nightmare barrage of field-filling drums punctuated by the odd muezzin-ish call to prayer—given how fraught the material already is (brown-skinned desert peoples vs. The Man), the Orientalist tinting is poorly thought through. Every time I went to the multiplex in summer 2016, I’d walk past an auditorium booming the thunderous punching-sounds foleys and Zimmer’s score from Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice , and it never failed to make my life a little more unpleasant. Five years later, the most cogent thought I emerged from Dune with was, “Hans Zimmer must be stopped .” More here .

Das hat jedoch einen anderen Grund, als uns vermittelt wurde: Dune scheitert nämlich in epischen Maßen daran, ein vielschichtiges, gut erzähltes erstes Kapitel für ein unvergessliches filmisches Universum zu präsentieren, welches über die Grundgedanken der Romanvorlage hinausgeht. Das zweieinhalbstündige Science-Fiction-Epos kann weder für sich als alleinstehender Film überzeugen, noch als Exposition, so wie es gerne manche hätten. Vergleiche mit Stanley Kubrick sind ebensowenig angebracht wie mit dem ersten Teil der Der Herr der Ringe-Trilogie. Dune wäre zwar gerne so imposant wie letztere, wie ein moderner Lawrence von Arabien oder wie Das Imperium schlägt zurück, ist am Ende aber vor allem eines: Emotionslos, generisch inszeniert, holprig erzählt, inhaltlich unterwältigend, mit schablonenhaften Figuren gefüllt und in seiner gigantomanischen Machart ermüdemd - inklusive des brachialsten Zimmer-Soundtracks, den ich je gehört habe. tema: Fotografia e efeitos visuais bonitos, mas não compensam
exemplo: Muitos reconhecem que a fotografia e os efeitos visuais são impressionantes, mas que isso não basta para tornar a experiência envolvente.
texto: In the end, Denis Villeneuve was all too right: Your television isn’t big enough for the scope of his “Dune,” but that’s only because this lifeless spice opera is told on such a comically massive scale that a screen of any size would struggle to contain it. Likewise, no story — let alone the misshapen first half of one — could ever hope to support the enormity of what Villeneuve tries to build over the course of these interminable 155 minutes (someone mentions that time is measured differently on Arrakis), or the sheer weight of the self-serious portent that he pounds into every shot. For all of Villeneuve’s awe-inducing vision, he loses sight of why Frank Herbert’s foundational sci-fi opus is worthy of this epic spectacle in the first place. Such are the pitfalls of making a movie so large that not even its director can see around the sets. How big is “Dune”? We’re talkin’ slabs upon slabs of angular concrete as far as the eye can see, spaceships that seem to displace entire oceans when they emerge from the seabeds of Caladan, and sandworms so large they could eat the Graboids from “Tremors” like bar nuts. Even yoked kings Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista look like tabletop miniatures when placed against its backdrops, as if cinematographer Greig Fraser discovered a way to shoot deep focus and tilt-shift at the same time. So why, for all of its unparalleled immensity, does watching “Dune” amount to the cinematic equivalent of being handed a novelty-sized check made out for six dollars? Why is the scope of Villeneuve’s dream betrayed by the dull shallowness of its reality to the point that his film’s most astounding effects — which are every bit as tactile and transportive as those in “Blade Runner 2049” — feel more like optical illusions? Why does this “Dune” feel so small? ~this review continues on IndieWire~

texto: Difficile de réaliser que cette expérience se termine ! Dune a pompé toute ma joie, toute mon énergie tel un vers des sables. La seule chose notablement plaisante dans ce très long-métrage est ses plans : très jolis, beaux à voir. Bien que les costumes notamment bellement réalisés permettent de se projeter dans cet univers alternatif de fiction qu'est Dune . Malgré tout, ce film fut une torture et m'a renvoyé au jour qui avait déterminé le début de ma longue période de haine envers le cinéma. Sa lenteur, son écriture, son essence n'a pas grand chose à envier à Twilight , surtout au niveau du personnage principal. Pourtant, je suis surprise de le voir reconnu de façon différente que celui-ci ! Finalement, je préfère oublier cette expérience horriblement ennuyeuse (et ennuyante) — même si cela me sera difficile.

texto: Excellent cinematography and direction…however, this has to be one of the slowest and dullest movies I’ve ever watched for a franchise of this size. It’s easy to see why this story was long considered unadaptable for the big screen. The film has the difficult task of introducing multiple families, political factions, key locations, religious themes, and complex world-building, all of which are challenging to translate from the novel to film. Denis deserves credit for making such a dense and difficult story coherent, but I don’t think the pacing works. I understand that much of the film is dedicated to laying the groundwork for the sequels, but watching it often felt more like homework than an engaging introduction to this world. I admire the craftsmanship far more than I enjoyed the experience. 3/5

texto: Dune is great in every possible sense. The visuale are gorgeous, the sound incredible and the cast speaks for itself. But, at the end of its two and a half hours length, Dune had me praying it wasn't going to fade to black. Not without having even started its actual story. And just then it did, so I was a little upset. I don't think that this habit of making "part one" films is good. I rewatched LOTR The Two Towers a month ago or so, and it was beautiful. Without rewatching either the fellowship nor the return of the king (yes of course I know those by heart, but that's not the point!) Dune is not like that. It feels chopped, not complete; it can't stand up until something else will come out, and even then, it should only be watched as a prologue to that other thing. I don't think that's something I'd like to find in a movie. Nonetheless, I would suggest anyone to go and see, for it is a very nice experience.

texto: I really wanted to love Dune, but I didn't. Throughout the entire runtime I was waiting for one scene to hook me, to engage me in what's happening and allow me to immerse myself in the experience. But it never happened. For full transparency's sake, I read the book earlier this year and saw the Lynch film shortly after, so I went in knowing full well what the plot was and how another film adaptation handled the material. And while Lynch's Dune is riddled with problems in its pacing and plotting, there are things it suceeds in over Villeneuves latest endeavor. But we'll get there when we get there. The biggest problem in this newest adaptation of Herbert's seminal work is Villeneuves incessent gigantomania. When he said this film needs to be seen on a big screen, he was right, but I don't think any screen in the world will be able to make the size of this film look manageable. Every starship in this film is the biggest it can possibly be, Arrakeen, the capital of Arrakis, is an amalgamation of absolutely massive concrete buildings built almost on top of each other and the armies standing in formation seem endlessly big. Because everything is the enourmous size it is, none of it ever feels believable. When the courtyard of your palace is a massive concrete plain that stretches as far as the eye can see, but is entirely devoid of any markings, wells, walkways or any signs of life, they just look like computer-generated textures. When the ships are all huge grey blocks with no discernible characteristics or features, they just become big blocks that look artificially placed in an empty-looking environment. Dune is big because it is filled with literally huge structures and buildings and ships, but they never feel organic. Which is the next big issue. None of the sets the characters inhabit feel lived-in, or natural, or like they convey an actual world. Why Villeneuve opted for every building to be a grey slab with grey walls and nothing on them, I cannot for the life of me understand. None of its feels alive, vibrant, or remotely natural. It's all just copy-pasted textures that have nothing to them. Contrast this with Lynchs version and the lush round and gold features on the palace exterior and interiors, the beautiful ornaments and art-deco-looking elements. They have character to them, and they give a sense of personality to the area the characters are inhabiting. Villeneuves environments feel dead by comparison. Speaking of dead: To call the characters lifeless would be an overstatement, however, they do all have an air of imposed seriousness on drabness to them, that weighs down on the general atmosphere a lot. Never is there a sense of levity, of a character being content, and actually tender moments between characters are very sparse. The only actor that is allowed to have the slightest charisma is Jason Momoa, but even then he does not get the opportunity to let it shine much. Timothée is good at what he does, though he always looks like he's constipated. The rest of the cast has to abide by the general tone of the film, which is unflinchingly serious, to a fault. Again, Lynch was able to incorporate genuinely touvhing moments while condensing more story into less runtime, so why couldn't Villeneuve? All of these elements, the artifical scale, the lifeless set design, the one-note characters, it all leads to a very distant and cold experience. Never did I ever emotionally engage in anything onscreen, the film started and then it ended and I was left pretty unphased by everything. It's such a shame, because the book as well as Lynchs film both have spectacle and scale as well as emotion and very human moments. But Villeneuves Dune could have also taken place on an ice planet and it would have fit the tone of the film almost better. The main difference between the two films is that the newer really wants to take it's time and properly tell the story of Frank Herberts Dune. While Lynchs film tries to tell the entire story in two hours, essentially crippling it and leaving an overstuffed mess, the new Dune is intent on staying true to the details of what Herberts Dune is about. Except for the fact that there is still a lot missing. Not just details and single exchangeable scenes, but actual plot threads that fans liked (I know I'm not the only one upset over the plot line about the investigation into who the traitor is missing). So this new Dune is longer than the old one, and only tells half the story, but because the plot is decelerated so much the 150 mins feel like 240. The first hour of this film drags for very long, since exposition in reading is easier to digest than exposition in film, especially when in film it is just delivered through dialogue. At the same time, so much happens in this first movie already, that thinking about having to go see another one like this feels like a chore. It still feels overstuffed. Overall, this is definitely the better adaptation of the book Dune, though it is not finished yet. The second part is going to be far more interesting than the first, so I'm keeping my hopes up. In conclusion, while conceptually more mature and structured better than previous iterations, Villeneuves first Dune film can't help but bury its great base material under heaps of comically oversized imagery (Hans Zimmers oppressive and incredibly loud score only makes this film heavier and clunkier), an atmosphere that is way to stern and self-important for its own good and an approach to its base material that is taking its time, which has two sides, as it allows for more detail and clearer themes, but at the same time still seems like its barely managing to hit all the story beats before credits roll. This Dune needed more refining in a lot of places, and overall, its not bad. It's just not as good as everyone wanted it to be. I don't want to seem like I hated this film, so here are a list of things I liked: The cinematography largely supported the narrative quite well (though also succumbing to the aforementioned gigantomania) and generally looked pretty good. The CGI is entirely seemless (except for the artifical building exteriors and interiors). Everyone in the cast is sexy as fuck. The story of Dune is finally getting a worthy adaptation, though it is a flawed one. Might see this Dune again soon, might change my mind.

exemplo: A trilha sonora e o som são frequentemente elogiados como imponentes e capazes de elevar a experiência visual, embora alguns considerem o som excessivamente alto ou intrusivo.
texto: 他，回來了！Denis Villeneuve用熟悉的「慢條斯理」，來處理這份難以搞定的佳餚，手法幹練卻不失細膩之處，以一個沒看過小說的視角帶入，確實有難以消化的難處，但本片不至於像諾蘭那樣具有「干擾性」，而是可以輕易地貼近角色來了解架構的「引導」，然而，本片的弱點，也正是因受到原著及商業類型的束縛，導致成品流露出虛假與流於表面，最終成為另一部虎頭蛇尾的鉅作。題外話，如果你真要體驗到本片的壯觀，拜託去IMAX或ATMOS廳體驗，那種震撼與感動交織而成的「屏息」，難以形容。 《沙丘》算是維勒納夫中段班的作品，或許是因為有改編難度的壓力，整體看上來還是綁手綁腳的，不像《異星入境》與《銀翼殺手2049》那樣「放得開」，但他的導戲功力已達頂峰，大場面的調度讓人驚嘆連連，龐大的世界觀他也能處理得毫無匠氣、游刃有餘，從沙漠瀰漫的危險感，到室內空間的窒息感，都能捕捉到其深刻之處。劇情基本遊走在殖民與天選之子上，然而，劇本的空泛台詞與過度簡化，多少還是影響了兩個主題的力度，裡頭的傳承與戰勝恐懼的意象，則因為情節的不穩定，與兒戲般的轉折，讓這象徵意義變得薄弱，只剩「說出來」的表面意義。 說實話，如果沒了這群演員的表現，本片的角色塑造絕對會崩塌，裡頭我最愛Rebecca Ferguson的演出，她將眼淚化為角色的痛苦展現，母性的光輝清晰可見，隱忍與噴發的情緒拿捏得宜。漢斯季默，宛如為電影戴上一層淒美的面紗、穿上悲壯的戰衣，人聲總是能帶出電影最唯美的一面，可惜配樂的編排使整體情緒過滿，導致配樂干擾了劇情進行與情緒延展，人聲則因為頻繁的出現，給人煩躁的印象。聲音設計著實令人難忘，爆炸與打鬥的聲音富有層次感，衝擊力更是做得恰到好處，可惜，高亢配樂的過度氾濫，讓音效展現不了真正的實力。 《沙丘》在我看來，就是部相當適合大銀幕的作品，場面調度無懈可擊、音效特效傑出無比，創造出一場宛如《星際大戰》的視聽享受，可惜這場史詩，敗在劇情的單薄，支撐不了片長與大場面的輸出，《魔戒》之所以能支撐得了三個小時的打磨，就是因為劇本的可塑性及魅力，才能讓情緒持續延展下去，但《沙丘》犯了一個錯誤，就是用過多的篇幅來「介紹」，及彆扭的角色塑造，使電影少了收放自如的情緒，及大小場面切換的流利，更少了角色之間激盪的火花。 但這個缺點，仍無法改變本片是商業巨作的事實，Denis Villeneuve用極為藝術與富有情調的氛圍，讓影片既有沙漠的粗曠，也有人性的細緻，這，正是維勒納夫電影之所以吸引人的所在。然而，這只是《沙丘》的第一篇章而已，接下來，還有許多寶藏等著維勒納夫來挖掘，希望這告一段落的時間，能讓Villeneuve適應商業片的呈現。最後，一顆星給場景設計及特效的絕美，一顆星給眾星雲集的卡司，一顆星給Denis Villeneuve純熟的導戲功力。

texto: Obviously great on a technical level, but I had major issues getting invested in Dune. I think it comes down to the characters and the world of Dune not being very interesting to me. It’s so desolate and empty, and I honestly felt like there was no point of being alive if you lived in this world! Like if anyone died, what are they missing out on? David Ehrlic described the movie as lifeless I believe, and I’ll have to agree :/ is there any chemistry between any of the characters? Not really! The world of Blade Runner, LotR, Harry Potter and so on, are much more fascinating and fun to explore! This movie for sure had some incredible worldbuilding, I just didn’t care about the world and the characters in it! The evil guys felt pretty generic and so did Timothee’s “the One” character! I honestly don’t care if the good guys or the bad guys win! Now the positives! Incredible costume design, visual and practical effects, sound design and so on! 100% a great cinematic experience! I liked Timothy Chalamet and Jason Mamoa! A few exciting scenes! I think my favorite thing about it, is how analog it felt! It felt dirty and real, like the opposite of a glossy Marvel/Netflix movie! Loved that! I’m sure there’s lots of visual effects in Dune, but it doesn’t feel like it! I was hoping to feel horrible about having to wait however long for a sequel, but I kinda don’t feel much! I’m definitely rooting for the movie to get a part 2, and I’ll for sure be there to watch it in theaters! But I’m not sure I’ll ever rewatch part 1 at home! (Damn, the movie is over 2.5 hours, and I already feel like I don’t remember much of what happened. Like nothing really mattered.)

texto: Dune is great in every possible sense. The visuale are gorgeous, the sound incredible and the cast speaks for itself. But, at the end of its two and a half hours length, Dune had me praying it wasn't going to fade to black. Not without having even started its actual story. And just then it did, so I was a little upset. I don't think that this habit of making "part one" films is good. I rewatched LOTR The Two Towers a month ago or so, and it was beautiful. Without rewatching either the fellowship nor the return of the king (yes of course I know those by heart, but that's not the point!) Dune is not like that. It feels chopped, not complete; it can't stand up until something else will come out, and even then, it should only be watched as a prologue to that other thing. I don't think that's something I'd like to find in a movie. Nonetheless, I would suggest anyone to go and see, for it is a very nice experience.

texto: There are two overlapping narrative strands, the conflict between houses and Paul becoming acquainted with (/returning to??) the ways of the desert. I was ever so slightly disappointed with the swift buildup and resolve of the former. In the end, the imperial betrayal and setup of House Atreides was merely expositional, functional for the Lisan al-Gaib pipeline which this trilogy is clearly going to be “about.” I’m told that’s how they do franchises these days, but something about watching a nearly three hour long (and brilliant!) film only to have it end with “there will be a second one!!!” in big bright neon letters irritated me. In a way, the semi-forced cliffhanger ending undermined the  value of the otherwise very intriguing world-building, at least for me.  Lastly, I couldn’t help but cringe a bit at Chalamat’s Daenerys-moment in the desert

texto: VENICE 78: There's a scene in Dune's first act where we are introduced to yet another faction of people and for a single moment I was taken out of the film, tearing myself away from the bombastic, ear-drumming score and larger-than-life visuals to wonder, so then who the hell are these people? The moment passed as swiftly as it came, but it's emblematic of a movie that almost buckles under the weight of its own worldbuilding as well as setup for things to come. Almost, I say, because it doesn't succumb completely, instead coming out on top to deliver an experience that thrills as well as awes, even in spite of its stumbling blocks. In that, it's not quite Blade Runner 2049, Denis Villeneuve's masterwork, but it's also far grander than that film, in scope as well as ambition. With Dune, there is a lot of ground to cover. The book has often been said to be "unfilmable", and it's easy to see why: its world is vast, its factions numerous, and its story incredibly dense. Because of this, the movie - billed as "Part One" on its opening title screen - only covers the first half of the book, opting to leave the latter half to a promised sequel. That's a gamble, because Dune spends so much time setting up its world and conflicts that if this doesn't get a follow-up, it would be infinitely frustrating: by the time the credits roll, the story's far from over. In many ways it feels like we're just getting started. This is where Dune will almost certainly divide people. Some may feel it's too much setup and not enough payoff; especially in the first half, viewers may experience the same thing I did in the aforementioned scene, to momentarily be taken out of it as they try to process this new influx of information. There's also the chance that people will feel disappointed by the end of the film, because it hinges a lot of itself on the promise of more to come: Zendaya, for instance, doesn't get all that much to do here, and the climax might be smaller-scale than some are hoping (though it really works on a narrative level). That's not to say the worldbuilding and setup are bad or unnecessary, in fact quite the opposite: there's just a lot of it. However, where Dune stumbles through these narrative shallows, if you allow it to find its footing as the sweeping political saga that it is - "Game of Thrones in space" as it's often called, though that comparison only applies insofar as it's about noble houses vying for control in a game of courtly intrigue, backstabbing, and all-out war - it absolutely wows, not just on a story level, but also visually as well as auditory. Rolling dunes, spaceships falling out of orbit, spice flowing through the air and sandworms filling the screen... its world of Arrakis and the noble houses of Atreides and Harkonnen are beautifully put to screen and sound, with a grandness to them that one so rarely finds in cinema anymore. The score by Hans Zimmer is terrific and cinematographer Greig Fraser has a beautiful eye on where to put the camera. The cast, too, gives it a Shakespearean feel: among others Oscar Isaac, Rebecca Ferguson, Stellan Skarsgård (in terrific make-up), and especially Timothée Chalamet and Zendaya (when she's in it) grace the screen beautifully. With this film it's clear that Villeneuve isn't afraid to give everything from its actors to its towering spacecrafts, to the grains of sand on Arrakis the attention they deserve. Looking back on the film now, a few days after I've seen it, I am strongly reminded of those history classes when the teacher starts telling a story, and at first you're not sure where it's going and there's a lot of information being thrown at you, but by the time the bell rings you're so invested that you don't want to leave, and you cannot wait for the next class - or, in this case, movie. I just hope Villeneuve gets to make it.

texto: A fascinating ‘what would you do if...’scenario is the jumping off point into an exploration of masculinity, the meaning of family and the institution of marriage in this well executed slow burning relationship drama from Sweden. There’s some great snow photography (coupled with an effective soundtrack) but the pacing suffers as the film dwells on them a tad indulgently. Surreal diversions in the script, thought-provoking though most of them can be, makes the film feel arty but some of the more head scratching ones are trimmable, especially the ending could do without the clunky metaphorical epilogue. An original and poignant film but at 2 hours, the intrigue wears off a little towards the end.

texto: Si l'instinct s'éduque, jusqu'à quel point la panique est-elle tolérée dans un cadre éthique d'accord de responsabilités ? La société dénature-t-elle le darwinisme social au profit d'un habitus d'héroïsme seulement loué, mais jamais enseigné ? Pourquoi l'instinct maternel et le rôle du protecteur sont assignés sexuellement et non nourris par les deux partis équitablement ? Un égoïsme altruiste existe-t-il dans la sphère de la morale ? Tant de questions posées par Ostlund restées sans réponse dans ce film en marge de ses travaux, héritier de ses films publicitaires sur le ski et pionnier dans ses satires sociales. Du bon (l'état de santé du couple montré dans les distances au miroir, la rave party sans musique) comme du moins bon (les sous-intrigues sans réel intérêt, Vivaldi qui nous est asséné sans discontinuer et sans plus vraiment de sens à la fin),  et le sujet des failles de la famille trop exploité par le cinéma scandinave doublé d'une proposition déceptive passé la première heure, me laissent face à une autre avalanche cette fois plus personnelle: me faut-il apprécier la beauté de ce phénomène (quitte à y retourner), ou fuir comme n'importe quelle personne sensée sauf un père de famille digne de ce nom .

texto: A single moment of crisis shatters the image of proactive, protective masculinity Tomas and his family have constructed around him. Force Majeure employs a clinical, alienating aesthetic of minimalist compositions that drain the Alpine resort of any warmth or coziness. The pristine white snow and hotel interiors are like a sterile laboratory. Every lingering frame feels hollow. And at the end of it all, after the denial, the gaslighting, the breakdown... Tomas, having experienced no real growth beyond earning the pity of his children, is offered a foggy 'rescue' scene that feels entirely staged. His wife Ebba allows him to play the proactive protector so he can reclaim the image of his so-called masculinity and their children can reclaim a sense of normalcy. This is his heroic moment, right? He's a 'man' again, right? Wrong. The film immediately undercuts this false redemption in the bus scene, where Ebba is once again the proactive one. She alone confronts the erratic driver who can't handle the controls of his own vehicle, and she alone gets him to open the doors so everyone can exit to safety, while Tomas sits passively. But, this time, he's willing to admit a fault to a member of his family instead of denying it to the point of breaking everything and everyone around him. Yes, he does smoke. Yes, he has lied. No, he's not picture perfect. Maybe there's some small amount of hope for him yet.

texto: A single moment of crisis shatters the image of proactive, protective masculinity Tomas and his family have constructed around him. Force Majeure employs a clinical, alienating aesthetic of minimalist compositions that drain the Alpine resort of any warmth or coziness. The pristine white snow and hotel interiors are like a sterile laboratory. Every lingering frame feels hollow. And at the end of it all, after the denial, the gaslighting, the breakdown... Tomas, having experienced no real growth beyond earning the pity of his children, is offered a foggy 'rescue' scene that feels entirely staged. His wife Ebba allows him to play the proactive protector so he can reclaim the image of his so-called masculinity and their children can reclaim a sense of normalcy. This is his heroic moment, right? He's a 'man' again, right? Wrong. The film immediately undercuts this false redemption in the bus scene, where Ebba is once again the proactive one. She alone confronts the erratic driver who can't handle the controls of his own vehicle, and she alone gets him to open the doors so everyone can exit to safety, while Tomas sits passively. But, this time, he's willing to admit a fault to a member of his family instead of denying it to the point of breaking everything and everyone around him. Yes, he does smoke. Yes, he has lied. No, he's not picture perfect. Maybe there's some small amount of hope for him yet.

texto: A fascinating ‘what would you do if...’scenario is the jumping off point into an exploration of masculinity, the meaning of family and the institution of marriage in this well executed slow burning relationship drama from Sweden. There’s some great snow photography (coupled with an effective soundtrack) but the pacing suffers as the film dwells on them a tad indulgently. Surreal diversions in the script, thought-provoking though most of them can be, makes the film feel arty but some of the more head scratching ones are trimmable, especially the ending could do without the clunky metaphorical epilogue. An original and poignant film but at 2 hours, the intrigue wears off a little towards the end.

texto: Si l'instinct s'éduque, jusqu'à quel point la panique est-elle tolérée dans un cadre éthique d'accord de responsabilités ? La société dénature-t-elle le darwinisme social au profit d'un habitus d'héroïsme seulement loué, mais jamais enseigné ? Pourquoi l'instinct maternel et le rôle du protecteur sont assignés sexuellement et non nourris par les deux partis équitablement ? Un égoïsme altruiste existe-t-il dans la sphère de la morale ? Tant de questions posées par Ostlund restées sans réponse dans ce film en marge de ses travaux, héritier de ses films publicitaires sur le ski et pionnier dans ses satires sociales. Du bon (l'état de santé du couple montré dans les distances au miroir, la rave party sans musique) comme du moins bon (les sous-intrigues sans réel intérêt, Vivaldi qui nous est asséné sans discontinuer et sans plus vraiment de sens à la fin),  et le sujet des failles de la famille trop exploité par le cinéma scandinave doublé d'une proposition déceptive passé la première heure, me laissent face à une autre avalanche cette fois plus personnelle: me faut-il apprécier la beauté de ce phénomène (quitte à y retourner), ou fuir comme n'importe quelle personne sensée sauf un père de famille digne de ce nom .

texto: Bleak, black comedy at its most deliciously uncomfortable and relatable. The avalanche sequence is incredible and an almost perfect short in its own right, playing out in one prolonged and detached take à la Haneke, but the drama is in how Östlund lets the aftermath slowly eat away at this seemingly perfect family, and Tomas is such a fascinatingly pathetic character who is also horribly relatable in some ways. Brings up so much to chew on about the nature of masculinity, marriage, base instinct and the discomfort of realising that when everything goes wrong you might not be the person you think you are. Hilariously vicious and ridiculously well-made.

tema: Roteiro fraco e falta de originalidade
exemplo: Muitos comentários apontam que o roteiro é previsível, sem sentido e se parece com obras anteriores da franquia. A narrativa é vista como uma reunião de elementos de várias partes, sem trazer nada novo ou interessante.
texto: Esto es el ejemplo perfecto de como no hacer un remake. Los primeros 20 minutos de película son perfectos, la mejor introducción para dar el origen al reinicio de la franquicia,  el problema es la hora y 10 minutos de película restante. Historia horrible, personajes horribles, diálogos horribles, no banco a nadie en esta película. Las referencias a las películas anteriores estan buenas pero lo hacen porque seguramente sabían lo mala que es esta película. Nosé, estoy muy decepcionado, me da bronca que películas mucho más viejas se ven incluso mejor que esta. En cuanto a Jason, está muy bien, definitivamente es el más hábil de toda la saga, aunque en diseño me sigue pareciendo mucho mejor el de Freddy Vs Jason. Creo que no tiene nada que no tenga las demás películas y no da nada nuevo tampoco, ni la hubiese visto.

texto: Friday the 13th and its main antagonist Jason Voorhees has been part of the American pop culture zeitgeist since I was a child. I knew about Jason and his murder sprees on Crystal Lake before I was allowed to watch, or wanted to watch, any of the movies. Jason hit a bit closer to home than other movie monsters like Freddy Kruger or Michael Myers because I grew up in rural Maine surrounded by forests and spent a lot of time on a lake at my Grandparent’s camp. The lake at night could be scary with its isolation, the occasional unrecognizable animal noises and limited visibility. If someone were to scream in the distance it’d be hard to pinpoint where it would be coming from because sound echoes off the water. On top of that, running at night in the woods is dangerous because of uneven ground and tripping hazards. It was easy for me to place myself in a “Friday the 13th” scenario. The lake also had its own kind-of-sort-of legend of a “crazy guy” who used to have a shack on one of the islands, the remains of the shack still visible. I don’t want say this is gospel truth as I’m going off of a vague memory and I don’t know what’s true and what’s exaggeration, but I remember thinking as a ten year old that if I did happen across an adult with ill intent out on the lake there isn’t much I could do except run and hide and I wasn’t that fast. My imagination built up the Friday the 13th movies so much there was no way they’d live up what I thought they were. When I finally entered the right of passage to watch horror movies at too young of an age…I was kind of relieved I didn’t find them that scary. Don’t get me wrong, I thought they were fun, but not the terror inducing experience I was expecting. My friends and myself would be cracking jokes the entire time. When we got to the original “Friday the 13th” (we watched them out of order) there was a running gag of going “Where’s Jason?” and died laughing when the killer turned out to be his mom (though the last scare was pretty good, highly influenced by Brian DE Palma's  Carrie’s ending I imagine). When it was announced that they were remaking Friday the 13th in 2008 I thought there was a chance they could make the Friday the 13th movie I wanted, but didn’t hold out much hope. While there are some absolute gems from the era, I consider the 00’s to be the weakest period for horror movies. They are typically sanitized by the studios for mass audiences appeal and can be cynically seen as resume padding for upcoming actors. I didn’t bother seeing it in theaters, but eventually caught it on VOD….and…I thought it sucked. Maybe I would have felt different if I was a teenager watching it with friends, but as an adult watching it by myself I was highly disappointed even with low expectations. Fifteen years later I happened to get a trial subscription for Cinemax because my daughter wanted to watch Kevin Smith’s “Tusk”  last Saturday night. Since I have access to a slew of movies for seven days I ended up watching “Poltergeist 2: The Other Side” and this movie yesterday. The reason being I knew I didn’t like it, but barely remembered it. The only elements I remembered was something about Jason growing pot and sex scene that was incredibly graphic, even by R-Rated horror standards. “Friday the 13th” is a paint-by-numbers slasher where a group of young and horny dummies get picked off one-by-one by a killer that just happens to be the champion of killing young and horny dummies. And my first complaint is about these characters we are stuck with. I understand there is a certain devilish glee in watching people with unpleasant personalities get murdered with creative kills, but I find myself unable to get fully invested in a movie if there is no one I care about. In this version of Friday the 13th the people are in two camps and neither of them are good. They are the people you’re not supposed to like being extreme jerks and the people you are supposed to care about are not jerks, but instead are f’n boring. The cast seems to be in their mid-twenties and there is no talk of them being either in high school or college, but still everyone is so immature I have a hard time believing these are supposed to be adults. Hell, even by High School and College standards they are vapid and shallow.. Take for example that there is a scene where Lawrence (Arlen Escarpeta) is at a party, but finds himself alone in the living room. He finds a clothing catalog, looks at a photo of an attractive model and starts the very beginning stages of…jerk’in it. In the living room. In the living room where people are still coming and going. And the model wasn’t even in underwear or lingerie. It’s just a lady in a nice sweater. He doesn’t end up cranking the yank because people come running into the living room to warn the others of the murders..but who thought this was a good idea?! Did they think the audience would be in the grips of suspense? And please keep in mind there is at no point prior where it’s established that Lawrence is like that. The whole sequence is just awkward and weird. The same can be extended for the aforementioned sex scene, which is worse than I remember and it’s not the sex itself. The intercourse happens between Bree (Julie Guill) and Trent (Travis Van Winkle) while Travs’s girlfriend Jenna (Danielle Panabaker) is out helping Clay (Jared Padalecki) find his missing sister Whitney (Amanda Rightetti). While we are guided by the movie to absolutely hate Trent it’s Bree who initiates the cheating. Nothing prior sets this up, as Bree was just a background character.It’s confusing why Bree would not only have sex with someone’s boyfriend at a party attended by the girlfriend,but record it on a camcorder. It’s also weird at no point did Trent object to having his infidelity recorded. It’s even weirder that this camcorder seems to come out of nowhere. It’d make more sense if Bree always had it on her, but she didn’t. And when Jenna and Clay do return to the cabin Trent and Bree’s betrayal is glossed over quickly and never addressed making me wonder what the point of it was. If there HAD to be a sex scene with Bree there were two other guys they could have used. Or at least imply beforehand that Bree and Trent were screwing behind Jenna’s back. While I have no evidence I can’t help but think that the group had done ecstasy prior, explaining everyone’s odd and hyper-sexualized behavior, but any reference to the drug was cut by the studio, but I may be giving the writers and director too much credit. I looked around and couldn’t find anything to back this theory up, so maybe the point is that everyone is an extremely stupid sexual deviant. And there is also a problem with the casting that I don’t think I’ve ever encountered with any other movie, most of the characters look the same. And I don’t mean everyone is just Hollywood beautiful/ possible Abercrombie & Fitch models, I was getting characters confused. Jenna and Whitney look exactly the same, so when Jason kills one of them I thought it was the other. Bree and Chelsea (Willa Ford) are interchangeable. Trent and Clay look like they’re related and early kill Wade (Jonathan Sadowski) looks like both of them. The only reason Wade stuck out is because he had on a stupid “F***K Christmas” shirt on (No explanation on why Wade hates Christmas is given). Even if the actors were good the script sucks with some of the clunkiest dialogue ever committed to the silver screen. Having recently gone through the rigamarole of script coverage and the demands for perfection getting your script made requires this script by Mark Swift and Damion Shannon makes me shake my fist at the sky at the unfairness of it all. The direction of Marcus Nispel is lazy and bad and he should be ashamed of himself. I tend not to be this harsh towards directors as movies are really hard to make, but Nispel just comes off as uninspired and bored. Granted, the past Friday the 13th movies are not exactly peak cinema, but the grit of their film stock and other signs of their low budgets makes the flaws palatable, if not fully forgivable. Even when they’re bad, they’re still fun. But this remake has a studio gloss that raises the expectations, its higher budget ending up being a weakness. It’s not a bunch of young filmmakers scraping together what they can to make a horror flick, using sex and violence as marketing gimmicks in hopes of getting a return. It’s a studio collaboration knowing no matter what they’ll make bank ( This movie made 93 million off of it’s 19 million budget) So when the acting is bad and the dialogue is bad and the characters suck and  the scares don’t  work, it really stands out. There is even one scene when two characters are running in the forest where you can tell it’s a soundstage. Despite my clear disappointment with the film there are two little things I can give the movie props for. The interpretation of Jason as a survivalist hiding in the woods is interesting and there is one scene with a character getting struck with a boat but not dying that was tense. It’s been over a decade since we’ve had an incarnation of Jason Vorhees on the silver screen. In 2025 we are going to be getting a television series called “Crystal Lake” from Television Producer Bryan Fuller (Hannibal, American Gods) which I have high hopes for given Fuller’s track record of quality content, but also reservations given Fuller’s track record of projects going sideways. We shall wait and see. If there is one thing that is clear, the mythos of Jason Vorhees and Crystal Lake is destined to endure even with all setbacks, failures, lackluster attempts and hollow studio cash grabs. As long as we know the fear of wandering too far from the campfire to engage in hedonistic acts, he’ll be there waiting. In conclusion….ch-ch-ch ah-ah-ah.

texto: Thus my Crystal Lake journey comes to an end (at least until October). I don't know if I just have Stockholm syndrome or if it was just anti-remake culture that was prevalent when I first watched this, but this movie isn't really that bad. It's still pretty mediocre, it's definitely not an Evil Dead (2013) situation, but in comparison to the following year's Nightmare On Elm Street reinvention, it might as well as be a masterpiece. This film has a real nasty edge with some properly gnarly gore, which does give it its own identity. It kinda surprises me that this is the only outing, which utilises a bear trap, especially because Part 2 sets up that Crystal Lake is bear country, however it does   lead to delightfully horrific results. I'm sure a lot of this is due to the filmmakers wanting to compete with the "torture porn" craze of the time, yet they do manage to hold their own well enough. The unfortunate over side to the grossness coin, it's how much aggressively juvenile misogyny is on display, leering at its female characters in a way only a Micheal Bay produced flick can. Similarly, the American Pie style sex comedy (outside of a few jokes) feels very tired and just unnecessarily unpleasant. The characters are a bit of a nothing burger, although not in a way significantly different than most entries and there's a few good performances scattered in. At first glance, the idea of combining story elements from the first four installments into one narrative sounds like a recipe for disaster, yet those movies are either a bit repetitive or rather simple, that it actually kind of works. The script wasn't gonna awards, the dialogue is far too clunky and there are dumb character decisions and contrivances galore, but some thought clearly went into it. Overall, if you stayed away from this because it's a 2000s horror remake, first of all... Fair. Nonetheless, you can do much much worse.

texto: This might be my biggest Friday the 13th hot take, but this is the best one. Not The Final Chapter or Jason Lives. And it's because Jason kinda kicks ass in this one. After 11 movies, Jason is finally, finally scary. He's actually intelligent in this one, having a tunnel system and setting traps and using bait and stuff, and (as much as I do like Kane Hodder) Derek Mears is the most physically imposing Jason we've ever gotten. I mean he actually runs. It took 12 movies but we finally get a Jason who doesn't just saunter everywhere. All that, plus the score kinda goes hard, and some of the characters are actually likeable in this one (even if some of them are really not). So yeah, maybe I'm just crazy, and i'm still not saying it's a great movie by any means, but it is the best of all the Friday movies. But I guess that probably says more about the series as a whole than this particular movie 🤷🏼.

texto: So here's the thing, most Friday the 13th films are average. As a series, it doesn't have incredible lows like The Curse of Muchael Myeys or Freddy's Dead, nor the spectacular rebounds like H20 or New Nightmare. It is a series that has remained consistently okay. And that's more or less what this is, another okay entry in the Friday the 13th series. It has all the sex and violence that you expect—actually, a bit more sex than you'd expect for 2009—but doesn't really do much to change up the formula. Ironically, not changing the formula is probably this movie's biggest strength. It's the 12th Friday the 13th movie, and it feels like a Friday the 13th movie. There are some changes that work, some that don't, but overall just an average slasher with a handful of memorable scenes makes for a fairly enjoyable experience if that's your thing. Which weirdly makes it possibly the best of the major horror franchise reboots. Friday the 13th never had the subtext of The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, the quiet suspense of Halloween, or the playful creativity of Evil Dead or A Nightmare on Elm Street. To put it bluntly, there just wasn't really much to fuck up.

texto: This is my #10 film in this franchise. I think some of the kills are good but I don't think the characters are entertaining and I don't have fun watching it. I usually skip it during marathons and never return to it as a standalone. I am not sure what it is about horror since 2000 but most of it has never worked for me. I have watched dozens of horror films of varying budgets and sub-genres released in the past 26 years and about 90% just fall flat for me. I am not going to claim they are not scary, not only is that subjective, but the fact is that I haven't been scared by a film since the age of 12 in the early 90s, so it is irrelevant. "I don't believe in the idea of good films and bad films. There are only films one likes and films one does not like. Neither is an objective measure of quality and consensus is not an objective fact. Guilty pleasure films are not a thing, never apologize for enjoying the films you enjoy, explanation and justification for ones preferences are owed to no-one.  I don't appreciate, endorse, or condone the use of terms such as elevated or prestige, these are just extensions of the good/bad consensus fallacy. They are reductive and dismissive snobbery and say more about the person using them than the films to which they are being applied. And now you know me" - Erobus Lycurgus

texto: Friday the 13th (2009) was my first experience with the franchise, and honestly, I had a great time with it. It doesn’t try to reinvent the slasher genre, but it knows exactly what it wants to be, and it delivers an entertaining ride from start to finish. Clay was easily my favorite character. Unlike many slasher protagonists, he isn’t just trying to survive—he’s determined to find his missing sister, and I loved how he never gave up on her. I also appreciated how protective he was of Jenna, which made him someone I genuinely rooted for. Trent was easily my least favorite character. His arrogance and attitude made him impossible to like, so his fate felt well deserved. I also liked that Jason wasn’t portrayed as a completely mindless killer. He follows a distorted logic shaped by his obsession with his mother. Whitney survives because she reminds him of her, which helps explain his actions—but it never excuses them. Understanding a villain’s motives is very different from justifying their crimes. The film doesn’t introduce anything particularly new to the slasher formula, but I honestly didn’t mind. I enjoyed it for what it was, and as my first Friday the 13th film, it definitely made me interested in the franchise. Sometimes a classic formula is all you need when it’s executed with confidence.

texto: Looking at the Rotten Tomatoes score and other reviews for this Friday The 13th remake, it seems like most people pretty much hated it. But I actually really enjoyed this movie and had a fun time with it. I like how this remake wasn't just a complete copy and paste story of the original movie. They swiftly establish the lore and cover Pamela Voorhees' story in the opening credits which I really appreciate because whilst Pamela is the OG killer, with this franchise, everybody wants to see Jason . Also, the birth of the iconic hockey mask is shown nicely here. One of the most memorable things about this remake is that it doesn't waste any time getting to the action and kills and it sustains this energy throughout the movie. The opening sequence is one of the best I've ever seen in a horror movie. Just that sequence alone would make for a great Friday The 13th short film. It's absolutely brutal and incredibly effective. The rest of the movie continues like this. The kills are so brutal and gloriously nasty, especially that opening sleeping bag kill. Derek Mears as Jason Voorhees is probably my favourite portrayal of Jason in the franchise. He's brutally terrifying, aggressive and monster-like throughout the movie. I also like how this Jason is smart and adaptable. His whole underground tunnel system is pretty clever and it explains how he's able to get around so quickly. I will admit that the writing is very cheesy and sometimes just straight up silly and it can be a bit distracting from the fun, darker tone but it doesn't really bother me too much. Also, I think a lot of people's biggest problem with this film is just how annoying and cliche the characters are. But I think that works for this movie and I mean, have the characters in this franchise ever really been that likeable? Overall, this Friday The 13th remake is a really underrated and incredibly brutal entry in this iconic franchise. With the cliche characters, silly dialogue, brutal kills, cool lake house location and Jason going into full monster mode, this movie fully embraces Jason's cult iconography. It's just a damn shame that this never got a sequel and nearly 20 years later, we still haven't gotten a new entry to this iconic franchise.

texto: I can see why this film is considered a classic , but it just didn't work for me. The opening battle, the massive wide shots, and the production design are genuinely impressive. Some scenes are visually breathtaking and still hold up today. Unfortunately, everything in between felt slow and uneven. The pacing dragged for long stretches, and I found myself losing interest more than once. The ending was the biggest disappointment, it felt rushed and lacked the emotional climax the story had been building toward. Instead of leaving a powerful impact, it ended on a note that felt incomplete. Technically, it's a well-made film with memorable visuals, but as an overall experience, it never fully connected with me.

texto: ANÁLISE DO FILME "GLADIADOR" O filme Gladiador, dirigido por Ridley Scott e lançado em 2000, retrata a Roma Antiga durante o período do Império Romano, acompanhando a trajetória de Maximus, um general romano que é traído pelo imperador Cômodo e acaba escravizado e transformado em gladiador. A obra permite identificar diferentes aspectos da sociedade romana e como sua política funcionava na prática. A narrativa inicia-se com a batalha das tropas romanas contra os povos germânicos. Após a vitória de Roma, o imperador Marco Aurélio convida Maximus a ser seu sucessor para combater a corrupção do Senado, alegando que Cômodo era incapaz de governar; entretanto, Maximus recusa a proposta. Movido pela ganância, Cômodo decide assassinar o próprio pai para reivindicar o trono, além de exilar Maximus e ordenar a execução de sua esposa e de seu filho. Maximus consegue fugir, mas, gravemente ferido, acaba desmaiando no deserto. Encontrado por comerciantes de escravos, ele é levado até Zucabar, onde é vendido a Próximo, um proprietário de gladiadores. Agora conhecido como "Hispânico", Maximus participa relutantemente de pequenas batalhas, atraindo os olhares da multidão por sua força e habilidades surpreendentes. Percebendo o potencial do lutador, Próximo o leva para o Coliseu, palco dos grandes eventos coordenados por Cômodo. Maximus vence a batalha final e se revela ao imperador, que fica indignado ao saber que ele continua vivo. Ao descobrir que seu antigo general estava bem, Cícero se encontra com Maximus para traçar um plano de fuga e libertá-lo da escravidão. Ao descobrir a conspiração, Cômodo manda matar Cícero e seus companheiros. Decidido a recuperar sua honra diante dos súditos, o imperador resolve enfrentar Maximus pessoalmente, ferindo-o traiçoeiramente na noite anterior ao combate para obter vantagem. Apesar dos ferimentos, Maximus consegue derrotar Cômodo utilizando a própria adaga do imperador. Em seus últimos momentos de vida, pede que seus companheiros sejam libertados e que Roma volte a ser governada sem corrupção. O filme se encerra mostrando Maximus no pós-vida finalmente se reencontrando com sua esposa e filho. Com essa breve análise do filme, podemos traçar paralelos entre o conteúdo do filme e a história real. Logo nas primeiras cenas, somos apresentados a uma característica marcante do Império Romano: suas guerras incessantes em busca de expansão territorial. Outro ponto crucial é o pedido de Marcus Aurélio a Maximus para que ele assuma o trono e erradique a corrupção do Senado, restaurando Roma à sua forma republicana original. Isso contrasta com a visão de Cômodo, que desejava que Roma permanecesse um império. À medida que a história se desenrola, testemunhamos o funcionamento do comércio escravista quando Maximus é capturado e vendido como gladiador. Isso destaca ainda mais outro aspecto do Império: a política do Pão e Circo, que desempenhou um papel significativo na ascensão de Maximus como gladiador. A crescente popularidade de Maximus alarmou Cômodo, levando-o a tomar decisões desesperadas que resultaram em sua morte. Review pra trabalho de historia

I can respect how good it is without feeling like it’s one of the greatest movies I’ve ever seen. Maybe the genre just isn’t totally my thing.

E mesmo que esse bunda do ridley scott goste de distorcer fatos históricos e manipular a história do jeito que ele quer, nesse filme foi no mínimo honesta a abordagem política. ah e é meio datado também.

texto: Gladiator passe deux heures et demie à construire des statues, puis demande à Russell Crowe d’être plus vivant qu’elles. Le Colisée, les armures, les foules, les bannières, la poussière : tout possède cette grandeur lourde qui donne au film une vraie puissance immédiate. Joaquin Phoenix, surtout, injecte quelque chose de beaucoup plus malsain dans cet univers de marbre et de gloire ; son Commode ressemble à un enfant enfermé dans un palais trop grand pour lui, avec un empire entier à disposition pour compenser. Russell Crowe fonctionne parfaitement comme centre de gravité. Il parle peu, avance droit, porte sa vengeance avec cette rigidité presque funéraire qui finit par devenir le langage du film. Mais à force de vouloir tout rendre mythique — chaque regard, chaque mort, chaque phrase — Gladiator finit parfois par confondre grandeur et emphase. Le film veut transformer un homme en légende ; moi, j’aurais parfois préféré qu’il le laisse simplement respirer.

texto: This is a really good movie, carried heavily by a tremendous plot. It’s not rewriting cinema or anything, but it’s well above the action movie average. Joaquin Phoenix’s stiffness originally felt like bad acting to me until I saw him in more movies and realized how deliberate of a character he’s portraying. Russell Crowe’s lack of emotion also felt stilted on first watch, but I’ve since grown to appreciate it. The music is very good, though it suffers from clearly being Zimmer’s prototype for what Badelt would help him perfect in Pirates of the Caribbean. Also, 2000’s slow-mo has a habit of looking abysmally choppy, and this film uses a LOT of it. Still, the resulting movie is much more often up than it is down.

texto: I fear I have lost the childlike wonder that makes stop motion inherently astonishing to witness.  Please disregard if that inspires the disgust within you that it does within myself. That being the case, this only really kicks my butt visually when a particularly inspired design or specific sequence crops up (THRILLED at the wood sprite assembling of ghostly eyes which continue to blink around its wings e.g.).  One would hope that the musical numbers would provide this fairly regularly, but A: the direction isn't especially spry, and B: WOW the songs are so bad lmao.  I almost feel bad for how crassly I put that, but it was truly a jump scare every single time one started how bland and tuneless they were. Elsewise, this is left to its kid's movie bonafides and this just sort of happens to be a really annoying one.  Winningly grim in spots, willing to wrestle with things like alcohol dependency and fascism and death, but also every scene is so direct and repeatedly underlined.  For the kids, I don't blame it, but it's not gonna capture me in the process, to say the least.  Really it's a bad habit of GDT's in general (such a funny duology, this and Frankenstein), but his best movies have so much going on visually that offsets it.  Just happens to be one that runs kind of flat in that regard, too.

texto: I.....am not feeling this one!  Obviously the stop-motion is incredible.  The whole world of the movie looks and feels beautiful with the level of aesthetic excellence I expect of del Toro. The character designs feel very distinct to this version and don't retread other versions I've seen; Death and the Blue Fairy are particularly memorable. However, as been the case for me with a lot of later day del Toro, the visuals are about all that work for me.  The plot is meandering at best; I like a lot of places the story goes (specifically the criticism of fascism), but it is paced in such fits and starts that it never comes together in a particularly cohesive or engaging way. It has a ton of cool ideas and moments and not a lot of meat. The big problem for me is...the music is fucking ass bro. I don't understand the choice to make this movie a musical with unmemorable songs and bad singers.  Like it would have been perfectly fine, perhaps even good without!! Such a bizarre choice! Like, I appreciate the artistry and the vision, I do. I will take a stop-motion film that doesn't work for me over CGI slop any day. But the bottom line for me is that it is just not that fun to watch or listen to. 🤷‍♀️

texto: 2.5/10 Themed Movie: - [ ] Animation August- Movie 17 Really didn’t work for me. The animation while technically impressive just feels so empty and lifeless compared to something like Laika. Voice acting feels phoned in on a lot of fronts and man Pinocchio’s voice is grating to listen to. I actually found Pinocchio as a whole really annoying. The dialogue is way too heavy handed. Characters just explain each others characters and emotional conflicts to the point where I couldn’t care less about what the film is trying to say. I also found the characters themselves really un engaging. I didn’t care for Geppetto’s loss. I didn’t care for the cricket’s writing career. I didn’t care for the relationship between Geppetto and Pinocchio because it doesn’t feel like it’s given time to develop overtime and just abruptly goes from them being at odds to loving each other to them being at odds and then loving each other. Oh and the songs fucking blow hot ass in this. Literally just dialogue with a little bit of rhythm to it.

texto: A wonderfully ingenious and aesthetically appealing display of stop-motion animation — and, to me, little else. Guillermo del Toro ’s Pinocchio strikes me as a frustrating waste of technical prowess — namely, the visual presentation and impeccable animation work — with such tepid, handholding material beneath the charming carapace. While worthy and multifaceted topics are indeed tackled, they are done so with no novelty whatsoever (beyond the aesthetic) and mostly with the depth of an entirely unremarkable children’s story. The subject of death is handled somewhat better by the end, but at that stage the damage was all done. With a slew of obnoxiously obvious allegories and a cartoonish simulacrum of fascism, the film attempts to juggle far too much for its feebly thin central storyline to handle; and these characters are so numbingly banal and paper-thin, I couldn’t care enough to get invested in them. Pinocchio himself is an obnoxious embodiment of the ‘innocent outsider can’t comprehend evil’ trope, which is neither new nor interesting when this barebones, and his relationship with Geppetto is as uninspired and one-dimensional. The Cricket is a perplexingly unimportant piece of the puzzle, and when he’s not around it’s easy to forget he is even in the film — and as a narrator, he serves no purpose; most of the time, he simply explains the obvious. As a comic-relief, he is simply irritating. Performances are also mixed to say the least — David Bradley is probably the standout, but what he has to work with prevents him from excelling any further; beyond him, I am not remotely impressed. Ewan McGregor, Tilda Swinton, Christoph Waltz and Burn Gorman are all capable of truly exceptional work — but here they are all wasted; and why bother casting someone as skilled as Cate Blanchett in a role that anyone could have played? As for the central child performance, I’m not a fan either — no disrespect to Gregory Mann, who I hope has a long and prosperous career ahead of him, but I find him grating and offputting in the role, with most of his delivery being stilted and inorganic. Overall, an all-star cast squandered. I’m well aware of the unpopularity of this opinion, and it’s not like there’s nothing redemptive here — the animators are obviously master craftsmen who should be commended for their massive efforts, and I appreciate this adaptation taking risks and trying something new with the classic story (though it does amuse me that, even when set in fascist Italy and focussing on the inevitability of mortal expiration, this version is not even remotely close to being as fucked up as the original). I love the concept of Pinocchio having the embodiment of death as a mentor figure, but this — like the other interesting ideas — is never expanded upon in any meaningful way. Plus, the stakes are completely compromised, and goalposts are constantly moved; several frustrating deus-ex-machina moments — like the avatars constantly bending or breaking their own rules and impossible feats being brushed over — prevent me ever taking the characters’ plights seriously. To me, this is an assortment of potentially brilliant individual pieces that can’t form a satisfying whole, with the disparity between the surface-level whimsy and the profoundly unremarkable tedium of the actual content being wider than The Terrible Dogfish’s maw. I totally understand those who extol the former element, but I just don’t meaningfully resonate with anything else.

texto: Front-loaded film that teeters off as it goes on, but I did enjoy it overall. On a technical level, stop-motion animation doesn't get much better than this, but this film's visuals are held back by its art direction. Besides Geppetto, all the human character look lowkey scary, especially Candlewick and Count Volpe (whose design is just repulsive, and not in a good way). Everything else looked great though, including the titular puppet. I'm particularly fond of the "biblically accurate angel"-looking characters (who, much to my amazement, aren't voiced by Cate Blanchett, who instead, voices the fucking monkey). While we're on the topic of voice acting, it was surprisingly not great. No performance stands out as being especially good or especially bad; they're all just kinda okay. Also, the songs really did add NOTHING to this film. I could forgive their lack of relevance if they were actually good songs, but they're not (except for Ciao Papa, which was really sweet, and a major highlight during the latter half of this film). Nothing - I can't believe I'm about to say this - comes close to the quality of the Disney songs. *heaves* *wretches* *gags* Speaking of things that add nothing, I can't understand the Ewan McGregor glazing in these reviews. Bro did assolutamente niente the whole film. To wrap things up, we love ANTIFA Pinocchio, but the story surrounding him is too messy, tangential and episodic-feeling to feel cohesive to me. The emotional moments really didn't hit the way they should've, nor did all the themes this film tries to juggle, even if I could see the vision. I would probably revisit it though, and I'd definitely recommend it for the animation and the novelty of its story and setting.

texto: “Terrible, terrible joy.” Finn Wolfhard trying to be British… Ariana what are you doing here? First off, let me shower the visuals with praise. I adore stop motion and it’s such a good medium with which to tell a puppet’s story. The locations are beautiful and filled with personality, I love the designs of the characters so much. Inside the Whale looks especially impressively gross, but my favourite sequences of the whole movie are the ones in the afterlife with the Blue Fairy, who has a killer design. The hourglasses and the lighting and the hares bantering over cards all feel like they were engineered to appeal to me specifically. So so so cool. Also, using Pinocchio to explore father/son relationships and then how that intersects with the state, especially during Mussolini’s Italy is just such a creative concept and I love it. I do have a few complaints that hold this one back for me. I found it a little irritating until maybe Pinocchio’s first death scene - after that it kicked into gear and I liked it a bit more. It didn’t help that at first Pinocchio was an utter menace, causing more damage than The Cat in the Hat . Like obviously I do not agree with the fascists but they were right Pinocchio needs to lock the fuck in. A lot of the characters kind of grated on me, but they got better after that. The dialogue the whole way through felt a little clunky though. The themes are presented well enough on their own, you don’t need to explain them!!!! As much as I love musicals, I found the songs irritating because the scansion was off and they were all too short to really get a sense of their purpose. Don’t make a musical if you’re not going to fully commit to it!! Criminal that the best song in the movie is saved only for the end credits. Desplat still kills it with the orchestral stuff though, no surprises there. It’s no Pinocchio: A True Story , but it ain’t half bad. Also this would go crazy as a Next to Normal AU.

texto: Acho que das obras do Del Toro (e olha que eu sou completamente apaixonado pela forma que ele vê cinema), Pinocchio, talvez seja a que eu menos gostei, claro, o cineasta tem eu seu currículo obras consagradas como: Pacific Rin, Labirinto do Fauno e a Forma da Água, que são filmes infinitamente melhores que esse aqui. Sinto que ele pode ter sido podado um pouco pela Netflix, por conta de algumas decisões de roteiro que explicarei mais a frente, mesmo assim, ainda é um pouco aquém daquele Guillermo que conhecemos. Eu tentei, tentei demais gostar desse filme, e olha que comecei a vê-lo muito porque eu achava que ele tinha sido um sucesso quando saiu, pode ter sido até, mas infelizmente, não funciona pra mim, e o principal (sem trocadilho) é o principal - Pinocchio, o menino de madeira é chato, tem uma voz extremamente fina que me irrita e, vou pontuar até detalhadamente o último ponto, eu não gosto das desobediências bestas dele, e por mais que eu saiba que ele acabou de "acordar" num mundo onde tudo é novo pra ele, tudo é uma coisa inédita e que ele tem que ver para entender, assim como os sentimentos humanos e até qual é o conceito de morte, eu acho muito subaproveitado aqui, outro ponto que me incomoda durante o longa e o que mais me incomodou na primeira aparição dele, são as músicas, nossa, como são chatas as músicas desse filme, por exemplo, a primeira canção que ele canta, ele perguntando pro Gepeto quais são as coisas e pra que servem, tinha tanto potencial, mas acho ela mal feita, não emociona e não tem nenhum "brio"; e por falar em brio, o único personagem que eu gostei, na verdade, a dupla, foi o Grilo e Gepeto. Eles dois juntos rendem piadas boas, porque é meio que um contra ponto do outro, há momentos muito bons entre os dois, como quando rolam frases como "Ele te ama, seu velho idiota, só que você não vê que ele só quer a sua aprovação, como pai" é simbólico, porque é quando o Gepeto se dá conta que ele não quer o Carlo de volta, ele quer o menino que já nasceu o amando, e são boas as conversas entre "dois velhinhos". Apesar de tudo isso, eu gosto de como o filme nos mostra que o luto nos leva para a decadência, como Gepeto fica após a morte do Carlo, seu primeiro filho, e aliás, já vamos pegar o gancho aqui porque quero colocar o ponto alto do filme e o diretor sabe muito bem fazer filmes assim e me faz chocar com coisas que parecem normais, mas não deveriam ser, esse filme se passa durante o governo de Benito Mussolini, então, você tem um contexto de guerra, em um texto que passa por ele e não é superficial, porque você tem um treinamento, ouça só: de crianças para ir a guerra, crianças emulando um confronto, com um fort, armas e formação. Ponto altíssimo aqui, porque a maioria das crianças nem entendem quando o pai fala "os aviões estão passando" e isso evoca o começo do filme, quando Carlo, filho falecido de Gepeto, vê um avião e fala para o pai romantizando-o "veja pai, é um avião" e seu pai meio que faz pouco caso, porque ele sabe o que significa um avião estar sobrevoando em tempos de guerras: tragédia. Pinocchio é um filme que mistura a fantasia com a descoberta, a morte com a tragédia, o luto com a inocência de uma criança, e que no fim, fica uma lição bonita, abrir mão do que você tem, pode muitas vezes salvar pessoas que você não quer abrir mão.

texto: What Del Toro lacks in subtly, he more than makes up for in heart and beauty. The long-told, well-established story of Pinocchio gets completely flipped around and played with in this 2022 wonder of a watch. I loved how relationship between Gepetto and Pinocchio gets recontextualised with the existence of Carlo (the religious imagery in that one scene being outstanding) & also changing the setting to Fascist Italy?! Sure, that’s kinda fucking rad! If I do have a criticism, it’s that after the first song, the musical numbers just got less and less good (a fact clearly recognised by the filmmakers, as the songs became more and more infrequent to the point of nonexistence). And honestly, that one song did take me out of it a lil bit 😅 BUT, it would be entirely remiss of me not to mention all the things I loved about it too: 1. The stop motion animation art form always boosts the quality of a movie in my mind, they always have a little magic to them and this is no exception. 2. THE CHARACTER DESIGN?! OH MY LORD IT’S JUST FANATASTIC! So many times, I felt my jaw drop to the floor whenever a new character was introduced. 3. STACKED CAST (in a good way). 4. Grief really do hit different. 5. I had a really nice time watching it with Elz. 6. A wonderfully beautiful ending, that can be improved upon in no way, shape, or form. 7. I LOVE YOU EWAN MCGREGOR. And so forth. Fun ol’ watch, and AI could never make something so beautiful and expressive.

texto: Um filme COVARDE Na sua busca do choque pelo choque, é o que Villeneuve se propôs aqui. Sua visão estéril sobre um filme, que por escolha própria, quis se ambientar em um local recheado de complexidade há 1000 anos, é pobre, rasa, fraca. O medo de entrar 1% na política fez o filme caminhar sobre uma pilha de coincidências até desembocar no "ápice" do filme. O fundamentalismo religioso é o cerne da violência que separa filho da mãe, que acaba com vilarejos milenares, que est*** mulheres e crianças com mais ódio e crueldade por volta dos anos 50', no oriente médio, isso não podia ser tocado no filme, porque implicaria culpa ao ocidente e Denis não tem essa coragem. O dito só precisa da locação, da língua e do povo, para que o OCIDENTE asissti-se aquilo tudo como - CENÁRIO - aonde se passa a tragédia e logo conectasse o pensamento com o que fomos ensinados sobre qualquer lugar do Oriente Médio: SÃO BÁRBAROS, POVO AMALDIÇOADO POR DEUS. Então a covardia, o medo, seu tom pasteurizado e apolítico construiu Incêndios, um filme covarde que busca o choque pelo choque, que o trauma é só uma escada pra te tirar um "NOSSA" no final. O filme é tão pobre é recheado de fatias de nada com coisa nenhuma, que se você reassiste, caso você tenha interesse (acho muito improvável), ele fica NADA. O filme poderia ter se passado em qualquer lugar, em qualquer época, é tão genérico, tão desconectado de tudo, que tanto faz se se passa em Ourinhos, Hamburgo, Xangai, New Jersey, tanto faz. Ele é neutro, ele apolitico, ele é covarde (de novo, muito covarde), o choque pelo choque, tudo pelo seu final, que nem é tão chocante assim. Um filme sem nuance, sem brio, sem força, sem alma

texto: Jour 12 pour voir le top 100 Letterboxd Dans un pays imaginaire, après une guerre de religion, les enfant d'une mère ayant vécu ce fameux conflit tente de retrouver leur père et leur frère caché. Ce film aurait pu montrer les horreurs commises dans les deux camps, tout en mettant en évidence l'absurdité de ces conflits et de la haine qu'ils engendrent. MAIS… Il ne faut visiblement pas brusquer le monde du cinéma. Alors, plutôt que de mettre les deux camps sur un pied d'égalité, on va s'attaquer à ceux qui ne disent rien. Je vous laisse deviner ? ( NON ) Les Chrétiens. On a donc un film qui imagine un pays, qui suggère l'appartenance musulman de l'un des camps ( Clairement inspiré du Liban) mais qui, pour l'autre, n'hésite pas à multiplier les références chrétiennes : la Vierge Marie sur AK47 après avoir abatue de sangfroig un bus entier d'innocent, des croix montrées à plusieurs reprises, des discours chrétiens entre deux scènes de torture, etc. Alors oui, le film montre des atrocités commises par différents camp. Mais pourquoi insister autant sur l'iconographie chrétienne lorsqu'il s'agit de représenter la violence ? à force, cela mes un noms simple a retenir sur ces atrocité " Le christianisme ". Et c'est justement ce qui me dérange : si le but était de dénoncer les horreurs d'une guerre de religion, pourquoi ne pas donner la même place aux symboles et à l'identité religieuse des deux camps ? Pour votre gouverne, 4849 chrétiens ont été tués dans le monde en 2026, dont 93% en afrique, selon les chiffres d'Open Doors. Ce film aurait dû faire beaucoup plus de bruit. Edit : 4800 comme le nombre de personne qui on mis 2 etoile a ce film ;)
