texto: ????????? The “gotchya” here being incestuous rape is so insane when the viewer would literally have NO WAY of putting it together because they used the same actor to depict a 15 year old and a 40 year old. There is no possible way the viewer can suspend their belief when the person we see commit the violence to The Woman Who Sings is LITERALLY A GROWN 36 YEAR OLD MAN. i just feel like i’ve had a really bad magic trick done in front of me that took 2 and a half hours of my life. I was actually really into this at first. I could feel some form of the twist burgeoning from the beginning of the second act, but actually just wtf???? It’s not even a “gotchya” it’s more of if they’d simply casted someone who even slightly resembled a young man or teenager I would have been able to make the connection without being explicitly told. The entire plots crumbles into nothing here. Look, the film was shot beautifully. Like I said i was invested, but In the end we have a lukewarm apolitical take that uses Arab lives as collateral for some “family is One” “Love thy neighbor as your brother” shit. Complete ignorance of the ACTUAL conflict that took place & is purposefully obtuse regarding the violence that was literally and TRUTHFULLY committed by Israel. I’m really really really not usually bothered by casting that may or may not be the “obvious” choice but the casting here literally obliterates this film. Nothing makes sense by the end of it. texto: Jour 12 pour voir le top 100 Letterboxd Dans un pays imaginaire, après une guerre de religion, les enfant d'une mère ayant vécu ce fameux conflit tente de retrouver leur père et leur frère caché. Ce film aurait pu montrer les horreurs commises dans les deux camps, tout en mettant en évidence l'absurdité de ces conflits et de la haine qu'ils engendrent. MAIS… Il ne faut visiblement pas brusquer le monde du cinéma. Alors, plutôt que de mettre les deux camps sur un pied d'égalité, on va s'attaquer à ceux qui ne disent rien. Je vous laisse deviner ? ( NON ) Les Chrétiens. On a donc un film qui imagine un pays, qui suggère l'appartenance musulman de l'un des camps ( Clairement inspiré du Liban) mais qui, pour l'autre, n'hésite pas à multiplier les références chrétiennes : la Vierge Marie sur AK47 après avoir abatue de sangfroig un bus entier d'innocent, des croix montrées à plusieurs reprises, des discours chrétiens entre deux scènes de torture, etc. Alors oui, le film montre des atrocités commises par différents camp. Mais pourquoi insister autant sur l'iconographie chrétienne lorsqu'il s'agit de représenter la violence ? à force, cela mes un noms simple a retenir sur ces atrocité " Le christianisme ". Et c'est justement ce qui me dérange : si le but était de dénoncer les horreurs d'une guerre de religion, pourquoi ne pas donner la même place aux symboles et à l'identité religieuse des deux camps ? Pour votre gouverne, 4849 chrétiens ont été tués dans le monde en 2026, dont 93% en afrique, selon les chiffres d'Open Doors. Ce film aurait dû faire beaucoup plus de bruit. Edit : 4800 comme le nombre de personne qui on mis 2 etoile a ce film ;)

texto: C'est loin d'être la claque à laquelle je m'attendais... Et je pense que c'est juste un manque d'implication émotionnelle Voir un film parler de guerre au Moyen-Orient c'est rare je trouve donc j'aime beaucoup le contexte de base. Oui le scénario est super, oui le twist est très glauque et bien amené, oui la mise en scène est excellente, oui la photographie est super travaillé et oui les acteurs sont bons mais je n'ai jamais réussi à m'accrocher aux personnages, à être emporté dans l'histoire horrible de cette famille ni à être choqué du sujet dont il traite. En fait le film passe avant tout par la théorie avant le ressenti (c'est pas quelque chose auquel je fais attention habituellement) alors compliqué de ressentir ne serait-ce qu'un peu de dégoût ou de choc malgré le sujet lourd et c'est bien dommage. Tous les moments qui auraient pu me marquer sont expliqués par du blabla. Je comprends toute la renommée autour de ce film mais je suis déçu.

texto: 該怎麼說呢，火燒車與結局確實震撼，但整體敘事卻感覺綁手綁腳，沒能更好地用鏡頭傳達，但也確實讓我很好奇原劇作的呈現，應該會比電影精彩很多吧？ 本片多次在觀眾試圖解讀影像之前率先透過某人講出媽媽發生什麼事，忽然失去探索影像的主導權，身為電影觀眾不免對此有些反感，且講完了還要再給你看事發當下的鏡頭，感到多餘的同時馬上瞭然不過是因為劊子手的臉很重要，觀眾要先看到他，後面才能產生劇本想要的震撼效果，但這種目的性極強的鏡頭手法卻讓人有點難以忍受。 火燒車那場戲的震撼度仍然是全場最佳，也確實帶出極有說服力的轉捩點，但下一幕就接到另一個時空女兒來到媽媽家鄉悠閒散步的觀光客模樣，又讓我惋愕怎麼能就此放掉火燒車場面的後座力，轉而把觀眾的情緒切斷？ 而全片都在用這種七零八落的平行敘事，看完後除了瞭解事態全貌與結局的震撼感外，在反思層面與鏡頭語言上卻蒼白得嚇人，無從得知媽媽後來是怎麼克服仇恨與兩個小孩相處的？知道真相後的媽媽是如何從震撼掙扎到寫出那兩封信的？小兒子是帶著怎樣的心情與思考後不小心脫口而出「畢竟我有那種基因」的？ 總之本片拋出了極其龐大的議題卻在影像上處理得零零落落、捉襟見肘，身為觀眾都不免為導演緊張得要命，也搞得「1+1=1」這種台詞像是用完即棄的震撼彈，炸完了什麼也沒能留下。

texto: Está bien. No me pegó mucho el plot twist, no se si me lo re esperaba pero bueno tampoco era una conclusión tan dificil. Creo que le sobra un poco de tiempo, se hace un poco pesada por momentos. En general no se, capaz porque le tenia mucha expectativa, pero no me voló la cabeza. Me quedo con la primera vez que vi oldboy Edit: Ultimamente no encuentro motivación para escribir análisis más detallados, pero creo que Incendies es una peli para ahondar mucho más y llegar a charlas super interesantes sobre ella. Se puede abordar todo, no solo el plot twist (que creo que la peli labura para llegar ahí más de lo que labura en estructurar la base de la trama) sino que todo lo demas; desde el drama político, la figura martírica que hacen de ella (cuando realmente no fue para tanto -aunque sufrió muchísimo-), el sinsentido de las herramientas de búsqueda, entre otras cosas. Recomiendo verla porque considero que es una película decente y que si te agarra desprevenido te debe re pegar; me gustaría que quien vea esta película sienta lo que sentí al ver por primera vez Oldboy, entonces sí, la recomiendo a pesar de que no me voló.

texto: Por sí sola, es una buena película. Habiendo leído la obra, no tanto. Sé que es tedioso escuchar críticas del tipo “la adaptación no es 100% fiel al libro” pero en este caso, me parece que pese a ser una obra, el texto original parecía hecho para el cine y no requería modificaciones. Entiendo que los cineastas toman ciertas decisiones, pero suprimieron partes muy importantes y agregaron cosas nuevas que no aportaron mucho a la historia. Casi todos los personajes perdieron gran parte de su profundidad: Nihad, Simon e incluso Nawal, todos parecían estar al servicio de la trama y girando en torno al “plot twist” y no se sintió el esfuerzo de desarrollarlos con humanidad.  Lo que más me indigna es que dejaron por fuera la historia de amor adolescente entre Wahab y Nawal, una parte tan natural, cruda y paradójica de la historia. Y ni hablar de la eliminación del personaje de Sawda: sin ella Nawal no hubiera cantado, y fue una lástima no ver ese vínculo tan puro y profundo. Reitero, todo estaba al servicio del plot twist. Enfin, es una buena película, pero si quieren sentir todo a un nivel más visceral y conocer una historia más humana, lean la obra de Wajdi Mouawad. (Odio que la gente piense que la historia es de Denis Villeneuve)

texto: Esthétisation permanente des scènes de violence qui désamorce leur portée dramatique ; dépolitisation complète de la situation à tel point qu'on galère à savoir où et quand tout ça à lieu juste pour se concentrer sur le drame familial (l'un n'empêchait pas l'autre surtout quand on voit la lenteur du film), aucun pays n'est cité alors que bah c'est la guerre civile libanaise quoi mdrr ; et la mise en scène de la révélation finale est totalement ratée. texto: C'est loin d'être la claque à laquelle je m'attendais... Et je pense que c'est juste un manque d'implication émotionnelle Voir un film parler de guerre au Moyen-Orient c'est rare je trouve donc j'aime beaucoup le contexte de base. Oui le scénario est super, oui le twist est très glauque et bien amené, oui la mise en scène est excellente, oui la photographie est super travaillé et oui les acteurs sont bons mais je n'ai jamais réussi à m'accrocher aux personnages, à être emporté dans l'histoire horrible de cette famille ni à être choqué du sujet dont il traite. En fait le film passe avant tout par la théorie avant le ressenti (c'est pas quelque chose auquel je fais attention habituellement) alors compliqué de ressentir ne serait-ce qu'un peu de dégoût ou de choc malgré le sujet lourd et c'est bien dommage. Tous les moments qui auraient pu me marquer sont expliqués par du blabla. Je comprends toute la renommée autour de ce film mais je suis déçu.

texto: Wow, I really don’t know what to say. Villeneuve is easily one of my favorite directors, and he creates such an expertly crafted story of family, war, and grief. The landscapes and visuals pull everything together so well, with static and lingering shots that really make you feel the emptiness and harshness of the world. It takes you through a multigenerational story, slowly unwinding the truth behind so much mystery. The first hour broke me, and I was out of tears for a while, but I assure you I would’ve had more if possible. Radiohead being the only songs in this is kinda hilarious, but it also works. As soon as the first song began I instantly recognized it and thought, “how does Denis have the audacity to play this after what just occurred.” It’s such a gruesomely real look into the world of war and how that shapes people. The narrative structure and time jumps, combined with the immense amount of travel, also help show the determination and desperation the characters have. It always gives you enough to understand and feel what’s happening without overloading you or cutting anything short. I do think the third act loses some momentum, and the ending itself is really emotionally deep but also a bit too coincidental and almost feels forced for impact. However, that really didn’t take away from the experience of watching this. It’s truly incredible and definitely something I have to rewatch. Wouldn’t be shocked if it rises to a 4.5 or even a 5.

texto: Esta película muestra la perspectiva de una víctima que se ve afectada simplemente por ser ella misma, por buscar la verdad y no dejarse llevar por el odio aunque se ve “obligada “ a cambiar de pensamiento, Es una película que pone la lupa la geopolítica y sobre cómo los conflictos terminan afectando a personas que, como la protagonista, no los han elegido. El hilo de la historia no comienza porque ella haya hecho algo malo, sino porque, en muchas ocasiones, no somos nosotros quienes decidimos nuestras batallas desde el principio. Poco a poco, las circunstancias nos obligan a formar parte de ellas, cuando lo único que buscábamos era una vida estable, tranquila y poder creer en algo que realmente tuviera valor.

texto: i didn’t like this. i found this movie to be confusing and a bit cringe at times. i didn’t like the fake sequences that occurred throughout the movie. the first time it happened was okay, when arthur imagined being in the crowd and getting called onto the stage at the murray talk show, because they cut back to reality straight after it. but the other times were annoying, like the fake dates he went on with his neighbour or him visiting a younger version of his mum after finding out that he was adopted. i found it all too confusing when i didn’t know what was real and what was fake. i really didn’t like when arthur read his mum’s letter to thomas wayne and he finds out that thomas is his “father”. i mean, who is believing that seriously? a scene i found cringy was arthur’s stand up comedy gig when he couldn’t get the words out because he’s constantly laughing. it felt forced and was tedious to watch. the last 30 minutes of this movie were really good. my favourite part was the talk show scene. i loved the steady build up to murray franklin’s death. i also liked that they showed bruce wayne’s parents getting killed, cool little touch considering this isn’t a batman movie. overall, joker is a bad movie, and the last 30 minutes save it from being a terrible movie.

texto: Temu Heath Ledger A pretty good summary for this film is “What if Taxi Driver and The Dark Knight had a child and it had 0 personality? Todd Phillips really tries to create a tribute to Scorsese, but as War Dogs fails to do it, so does Joker.  Todd, again is carried into mediocrity by an amazing performance by one of the greats of our generation, who wastes his talent in this. Joaquin Phoenix puts a really good performance, in my opinion not enough to win the Oscar, thats undeniable, but his performance is clearly not enough to make this film any interesting and nowhere near the performance Heath Ledger put for the real Joker. The writing of his character is also pretty pathetic, a character that has always had political/social motivations gets diminished into a depressed maniac that begins a killing spree because his mom lied to him, that is just as disrespectful as it gets. The whole film feels like a bunch of shorts put together in order to create an overall story with no continuity or direction for the most part. In general, I'd say it's an Oscar bait and a film made for spectators that aren't willing to see the deepness in films, those who just want that served in a silver plate for them, leading to it having no actual real meaning and it feeling absolutely empty. The bizarre and bloody scenes feel like they just serve one purpose, camouflaging how mediocre the rest of the film is, I guess thats another attempt to pay tribute to Taxi Driver, but Taxi Driver is fantastic even without these scenes. I really wish the film was better, because I believe Joker is one of the greatest fiction characters ever,who has been mistreated in a lot of films, ruining his potential.

texto: Le film paraissait beaucoup plus deep quand j'avais 13 ans... On voit que Todd Phillips a essayé de faire un film intelligent mais tous les thèmes sont abordés de manière superficielle. Le film montre un mouvement de révolte populaire mais sans jamais montrer les raisons de leur colère, leur idéologie, les dynamiques entre les classes sociales. Ils se battent contre "le système" sans jamais nous dire quel système sûrement parce que le réalisateur avait peur de faire un film trop politique. La maladie mentale est aussi représentée de manière ultra caricaturale, Joaquim Phoenix en fait trop, il se sent obligé de sortir des phrases ultra dramatiques ("Are you having negative thoughts 🤔? All I have are negative thoughts 😈") + musique triste pour bien nous faire comprendre qu'il va pas bien. Ducoup au lieu d'avoir un film intéressant sur l'intersection entre la pauvreté et les problèmes de santé mentale qui montrerait un vrai mouvement social avec de vrais revendications on a juste un film sur un mec qui se venge des gens qui ont pas été gentils avec lui parce qu'il est trop dark.

texto: Fór á þessa mynd í bíó þegar hún kom út og fannst hún alveg rosaleg. Það er eitthvað sláandi þegar maður sér hana í fyrsta sinn og hvað sem það er þá virkaði það 100% á mig. En svo fannst mér hún ekki skilja neitt sérstaklega mikið eftir sig, ég var hættur að hugsa um hana viku seinna. Hef horft á hana tvisvar eða þrisvar síðan og fíla hana minna í hvert sinn. Þetta er reyndar fyrsta skiptið í nokkur ár, og ég var að fersk sýn myndi kannski hjálpa mér að sjá aftur það sem ég sá í fyrsta skiptið, en hún gerði bara frekar lítið fyrir mig. Þegar ég horfi á hana núna finnst mér eins og Todd Phillips hafi alveg rosalega mikið langað til að gera mynd sem “hefur eitthvað að segja,” án þess að vera almennilega með það á hreinu hvað þetta “eitthvað” væri. Útkoman er mynd sem eiginlega fer bara í taugarnar á mér. En ég fílaði hana í fyrsta skiptið, það verður ekki af henni tekið.

texto: I recently watched Taxi Driver and I just watched The King of Comedy and having heard this was a bad imitation of those, I finally threw it on. My expectations were low, both with those films as recent points of comparison and considering movie's reputation. At first I found it merely tolerable, then for awhile I didn't hate it, and then I got to the finale. Yikes. Phoenix is doing so much in this and it's generally engaging. I get the accolades. He's acting, that is for sure! The film also looks very good! The score, though, is SO heavy-handed. It's just very dumb. It's just all so very dumb. Also: is this 70s-set so we can imagine Bruce has grown into Batman in 1989? Does Todd Phillips know that the 70s were not 20 years ago? === I take notes as I watch movies a lot of the time and most of the above was written before the big talk show set piece, and I both hadn't been spoiled on it but had an idea of what was going to happen and man it's just ugly when it happens. Ultimately this movie was just kinda nihilistic trash, huh?

texto: i didn’t like this. i found this movie to be confusing and a bit cringe at times. i didn’t like the fake sequences that occurred throughout the movie. the first time it happened was okay, when arthur imagined being in the crowd and getting called onto the stage at the murray talk show, because they cut back to reality straight after it. but the other times were annoying, like the fake dates he went on with his neighbour or him visiting a younger version of his mum after finding out that he was adopted. i found it all too confusing when i didn’t know what was real and what was fake. i really didn’t like when arthur read his mum’s letter to thomas wayne and he finds out that thomas is his “father”. i mean, who is believing that seriously? a scene i found cringy was arthur’s stand up comedy gig when he couldn’t get the words out because he’s constantly laughing. it felt forced and was tedious to watch. the last 30 minutes of this movie were really good. my favourite part was the talk show scene. i loved the steady build up to murray franklin’s death. i also liked that they showed bruce wayne’s parents getting killed, cool little touch considering this isn’t a batman movie. overall, joker is a bad movie, and the last 30 minutes save it from being a terrible movie.

texto: The superhero movie genre may be kind of cliched and derivative at this point, but I think that Joker is a step in the wrong direction. Joker is still a cliched and derivative film, it just derives from a different style of genre. There are things in this movie that are incredible. Joaquin Phoenix totally deserved a better movie than this. But I guess the problem is that it's just another entry into the same Martin Scorsese kind of movie, and it doesn't add anything towards that genre. I think everyone already knows that the divide between the upper class and the working class is a bad thing, Parasite literally told us that in a better way. As innovative as people say it is, it's still ultimately another Oscar bait movie that doesn't breathe any new life into its genre.

texto: No words can describe how this movie makes me feel. It’s a masterpiece. The acting, the story, the emotions. So much about this movie feels nothing like joker, yet by the end of the movie, you still feel like this is a perfect joker movie. I think it’s a really good example of how you can go off script and do something different from the original source material, and still tell a compelling story. Joaquin Phoenix plays such a great role in this movie it’s crazy. I think he’s easily the second best joker. No one beats heath ledger obviously. Joker is a brilliant movie about not just the coming of the clown prince of crime, but a heartbreaking story about illness. About how people around you can really break you and beat you down. Joker isn’t a villain in this movie because he’s mentally insane. Because there’s so many times in this movie where he’s a really sweet guy. But he’s a villain because that’s what Gotham made him. The people of higher power in that city don’t know how Arthur feels. It’s such a heartbreaking movie but it’s so good. And honestly if Batman was in this movie at all, this would be second place in my Batman lists. But I don’t think that’s very fair. Thank goodness joker never got a sequel

texto: This films manages to show, through the eyes of an outcast, how mad and sick our society is. The clown aren’t those who comes to light, accepting the label other attribute to them, but those who hide their true identity for the sake of their reputation and of their privileges. A society where everyone was born free, each one and the same measure, but where some cannot afford even the bare minimum to live with dignity, while others plan to buy a spare mansion for summer… A society where the weaker who asks for a better treatment is seen as a fool, someone to make fun of, and the mighty go on undisturbed, craving for more. ‘Joker’ is set in the ‘80, but it shows us a truth we still live nowadays: “we are all equals, but some are more equal than others”.

texto: "É impressão minha ou o mundo está ficando mais maluco?" Esse filme é simplesmente fantástico. Todd Phillips apresenta uma visão mais humana e profunda de um dos maiores inimigos do Batman. Em vez de mostrar apenas o Coringa como um psicopata que espalha o caos, acompanhamos Arthur Fleck, um homem fragilizado, solitário e constantemente desprezado pela sociedade, até sua transformação no símbolo do caos que conhecemos. Gotham é sombria, suja, violenta e decadente, uma estética que combina perfeitamente com os temas de desigualdade social, abandono e saúde mental abordados pelo filme. Joaquin Phoenix entrega uma atuação impecável, mergulhando completamente na complexidade emocional de Arthur e transitando entre fragilidade e violência. A história também mexe muito com a cabeça, lembrando Taxi Driver, com momentos desconfortáveis e situações que fazem o espectador questionar o que é real. Apesar do ritmo lento e da duração extensa, é uma experiência muito interessante. O roteiro, a cinematografia e a atmosfera são espetaculares, e o filme consegue fazer refletir sobre sanidade, realidade e a forma como a sociedade trata aqueles que são constantemente negligenciados. No fim, Coringa vai muito além de uma simples história de origem: é uma obra complexa, desconfortável e que realmente fica na cabeça depois dos créditos. Nota: 8/10

texto: I’ve always been interested in Christopher Nolan first big movie and now that I’ve watched it I’ve got some thoughts. I really do enjoy this concept of the main character having short term memory loss but the way they’ve done it in this movie made me confused. The movie decides to make the events out of order and for me I couldn’t help but not to be confused and having not a clue what is happening in the plot. If you ask me this movie didn’t have to be as complicated as it is and could have been simpler. I didn’t know where to put myself I don’t think this is a bad movie but I don’t think it’s for me. I think the acting is a good and it’s got to take a good acting to act like he doesn’t know anything or anybody and I think Guy Pearce did a good job in this role. The supporting actors are good I did like the scene with Carrie-Anne Moss basically saying she could use the main character however she can and he won’t remember. Overall I still recommend watching this movie as it’s not a bad watch and I can actually see me enjoying this movie more on a rewatch as I’ll be able to put the plot together a lot better.

texto: I finally watched Memento and it is one of Christopher Nolan's weakest films. Firstly I like the idea of the film, it follows a man suffering from short term memory as he searches for his wife's killer and to help himself piece the puzzle together he makes use of photographs and notes to remember key details. Now this is a fresh idea and something I haven't seen before but the execution was lackluster. The story and editing of the film is non linear. The film drops us into major plot points and goes backwards a couple of moments before that point to show us the events leading up to that major story beat. My issue is how jarring this while watching because you're confused half the time. Something major happens and then you're in a completely different scene that seems unrelated. I understand fundamentally it's to have the user feel like Leonard the main character because he has short term memory loss and throughout the film finds himself in strange situations he has no recollection of being in, but for me it made the film feel disjointed and difficult to comprehend. And the film's structure doesn't help with character introductions or development because the film introduces a character that knows Leonard but as the viewer you only get context of how they met later on, which makes it difficult to understand characters' motivations and why they behave the way they do. Another issue I have are the black and white exposition dumps Leonard gives us; they are misplaced and the black and white filter feels out of place. If the purpose of the film was to make the viewer as confused as the main character I'd say Nolan did a great job. The only positives of the film are Leonard's monologues. Most of the film is spent inside Leonard's head and Guy Pierce does a great job portraying his confusion and the struggles of short term memory loss and having to rely on notes and other people which could easily manipulated which is another aspect of the film I enjoyed. As Leonard tries to find his wife's killer you notice how the notes he makes and the people he talks to are unreliable and how he has to discover the truth when he can't trust anyone or anything. I love Christopher Nolan but Memento wasn't great.

texto: It’s not a bad watch (pacy, interesting, relatively entertaining), but I’d argue that it is a bad film. This has film school written all over it. It indulges in the assumption that it’s smart. In reality, it’s a simple plot made interesting through the reverse chronology. The stylistic choices were at an eye-rolling level of film school cliche (brooding scenes in black-and-white do not a masterpiece make). Like other Nolan films, I felt no emotional connection to this story. I was very aware I was watching a film, rather than feeling invested in the world of these characters. There’s no emotional intelligence in Nolan’s filmmaking, and so I find myself searching for positives in the technical aspects of his films. But I found the screenplay entirely overdone, almost written like a novel where everything has to be said rather than shown. The sterile acting reinforced the distance I had as a viewer from this film.

tema: Narrativa não linear e confusão intencional
exemplo: As reviews positivas frequentemente destacam que o filme usa uma estrutura de storytelling não linear que inicialmente confunde, mas que é parte da experiência e da imersão, colocando o espectador na mesma condição de confusão do protagonista.
texto: Christopher Nolan’s directorial genius elevates a linear narrative into a deeply entertaining one. By placing the audience in a constant state of disorientation at the start of every scene, Nolan masterfully forces us into the same fractured mental state as Lenny, keeping us thoroughly engaged. The awe we feel each time we piece together a clue—an ability Leonard is tragically deprived of—is brilliantly executed. We also see that the protagonist is constantly cautious about whom to trust. He suspects he is being used, and while this is true, the only proof he has to back his theories is the anecdotal evidence he has gathered himself. This is a puzzle we, the audience, are also trying to figure out for the majority of the film. Towards the end, we realize that he is indeed being manipulated: by Natalie for arguably pragmatic reasons, and by Teddy, who kills two birds with one stone by giving Lenny a purpose for living while also serving his own personal interests. Because of this shared confusion, the audience is led to believe that Lenny's truth is our truth. However, at the actual chronological end of the story, Lenny subtly reveals that he’s actively choosing to live for revenge. He desperately wants meaning for his actions, or in his own words: "I have to believe in a world outside my own mind. I have to believe that my actions still have meaning, even if I can't remember them." The true tragedy is not what he has forgotten, but what he actively chooses to bury. His inability to move on is not simply because he cannot make new memories, but rather because of his own active choice to forget the ones that don't fit his narrative. Teddy captures Lenny’s state perfectly: “So you lie to yourself to be happy. Nothing wrong with that—we all do. Who cares if there's a few little things you'd rather not remember?" This perfectly reflects the true message of the film: the choices Lenny has made since the incident are ultimately to blame. His willingness to lie to himself leads him to commit terrible tragedies just so he can live comfortably in a fabricated reality. He chooses to ignore everyone's warnings and run from the truth. Despite everything that is revealed, he willfully continues living in ignorance, perfectly punctuated by Lenny's—and the film's—final line: "Now... where was I?" before looping seamlessly back to the opening sequence.

Despite everything that is revealed, he willfully continues living in ignorance, perfectly punctuated by Lenny's—and the film's—final line: "Now... where was I?" before looping seamlessly back to the opening sequence.

texto: Estructuralmente es una película única. El guion es bueno, se nota bastante que está escrita por Jonathan Nolan y no por su hermano. El hecho de que descubras que la historia es una venganza a medida que la película retrocede está increíble, como también lo está que descubras que todo es una rueda mientras la trama avanza(?). Lo que siento muy muy flojo es la justificación que le da la película al personaje para seguir alimentando esa pescadilla que se muerde la cola. No te compro que lo haga simplemente porque necesita una mentira para vivir y blabla, hubiese preferido que simplemente fuese un ciclo sin fin de veces en las que es utilizado. Es decir, no me creo que sea tan metódico para absolutamente todo, pero luego arranque las páginas de su informe policial y tome decisiones enajenado sin poder apuntar las consecuencias después etc, etc. No sé tío, recuerdas todo antes del accidente pero empiezas a sabotearte a ti mismo… Tu mujer no murió, era diabética, estuviste interno, confundes tu historia con la de un cliente que tuviste… Simplemente no puedo comprarte que sea porque el prota necesita una excusa, no después de haberle visto tan metódico durante toda la peli. Otra cosa que no me ha convencido es los tiempos de almacenamiento de un recuerdo(?), no sé cómo definirlo, pero me refiero al hecho de que a veces la memoria tarde minuto y medio en olvidar algo y luego otras veces como 5, sobre todo con los nombres, conversaciones y lugares en los que se encuentran objetos y demás. Creo que eran detalles muy complicados de plasmar, y que no está a la altura del resto de guion. A pesar de esto, es una gran película, seguramente la mejor de Nolan, a pesar de ser su debut.

texto: OBRA MAESTRA Antes que nada, mis dieces a Christopher Nolan por sacar adelante un filme así, tan original e inmersivo que, por lo menos a mí, me ha mantenido pegado a la pantalla en todo momento. Si no quitas ojo y prestas atención a TODOS los detalles, esta película es una auténtica joya. Me considero una persona muy observadora, siempre intento que no se me escape nada, y esta película ha sido hedonismo puro. Es increíble como Nolan hace que sientas la ansiedad, el agobio, la tortura y la cárcel mental de no recordar lo que ha sucedido hace dos minutos, rodando la trama al revés. Esa manera tan única de meterte en la piel del protagonista y tan diferente de cualquier otra película: aquí no estás inquieto por saber qué pasará después, si no por qué ha pasado ANTES. Es como si te convirtiesen a ti en el enfermo durante dos horas, y ESO es lo que la hace tan brutal. Es cruda, es misteriosa y su estética me parece sensacional, así como las actuaciones, la fotografía y la voz en off. Todos los detalles y los giros están tan bien elegidos que no puedo sino apreciar y aplaudir el proceso creativo del auténtico rematado de la cabeza que ha ingeniado semejante puzzle. En el ámbito filosófico, moral y reflexivo de la película —película que, por cierto, sigue una línea similar a Shutter Island en su invitación al dilema moral, lo cual, al tener que darle al coco, me encanta— es curioso como los dos personajes, “Teddy” y Natalie manipulan al protagonista para conseguir lo que quieren, así como el protagonista se manipula a sí mismo y se cree sus propias mentiras… y tira para adelante, aun tras asumir la verdad, ¿o no? A destacar la genialidad de Joe Pantoliano —Ralphie en Los Soprano , actorazo de los pies a la cabeza, un virtuoso este señor— a quien tanto cariño tengo. También, por supuesto, a Guy Pierce, se da por entendido. Para que luego parezca que soy hater de Nolan. Reafirmo lo que dije en mi review de Tenet. Donde más brilla Nolan es también donde más flaquea, es como un vaso de agua que a veces se desborda (véase Tenet o la Odisea) y a veces se queda lleno a la perfección (véase The Prestige, El Caballero Oscuro o Memento). ¡BRA-VO!

texto: Dans la catégorie des films que j’aurais jamais regardés de moi même mais que j’ai vus parce qu’ils passaient à la télé, Mother! c’est celui auquel je pense le plus. Je le prends comme un film d’auteur qui cherche à dire un truc de très vrai mais qui le fait par la recherche d’impact tellement dérangeant que ça dessert l’œuvre. Au fond, c’est l’histoire d’un écrivain qui voue sa vie à l’écriture de son livre, et qui une fois publié le regarde être disséqué, analysé, jugé par le public qui ne connaît pas la personne qui l’a écrit, seulement le produit fini. La mère qui donne naissance à son bébé, et qui invite des parfaits inconnus pour célébrer sa naissance, et les inconnus se mettent à fouiller les placards, à faire comme chez eux, et a un moment le bébé tombe par terre et les gens mangent le bébé - Stop. Y’a des trucs qu’on fait pas. On met pas en scène un bébé qui se fait dévorer par une foule de sauvages. Et pourtant, si j’en crois le film, je fais donc partie de ces gens qui piétinent sa création. Mais il y a une difference entre faire comprendre qu’on saccage sa création et montrer un nourrisson se faire déchiqueter par une foule sous les yeux de sa mère impuissante et de son père qui refuse d’agir Et à l’époque quand j’ai vu ça, ça m’a carrément énervé. Comment ça y’a un studio qui met en scène un truc comme ça et ça sort en salles et c’est acclamé par le public? On touche pas les bébés. Y’a des limites. Pour moi c’est de la branlette intellectuelle d’auteur. Si tu veux faire du sensationnel, fais confiance à ton public au lieu d’aller chercher dans un registre aussi malsain.

texto: Day 1 of surviving my bsf favorite movies @ruyaarchive… I understand what this movie is trying to say. I understand the biblical allegory, the symbolism of Mother Nature, creation, worship, humanity, destruction, the cycle of creation and destruction, and all of that. I genuinely do. But understanding what a movie is trying to communicate doesn’t mean I have to enjoy watching it. Because honestly, for most of this movie, all I could think was: why the fuck is this man incapable of respecting his wife’s boundaries? From the very beginning, Mother is uncomfortable with these people invading her home. This is their house. Her safe space. The place she has been rebuilding and caring for. Yet Him constantly welcomes more and more people inside because he enjoys being admired. He doesn’t care that she’s uncomfortable. He doesn’t care that her privacy is being invaded. He doesn’t care that the people he’s invited are destroying the very home she has worked so hard to create. And that was the most frustrating part of the entire movie for me. I didn’t see some mysterious, fascinating, all-powerful Creator. I saw an incredibly self-absorbed man who desperately needs to be worshipped and praised by everyone around him, to the point where he is willing to sacrifice the person closest to him for it. And then the movie just keeps escalating. The guests become increasingly obsessive. The worship becomes increasingly disturbing. The house turns into complete chaos. And somehow, through all of this, Him continues to let them in. At some point I genuinely felt like I was watching a cult form around this man. People aren’t simply admiring him anymore—they’re worshipping him. They’re willing to destroy everything around them for him. And Mother? She is the one who actually creates. She is the one who gives life. She is the one who builds and nurtures. Yet she is ultimately valued for what she can provide, not for who she is. Her existence is treated as something useful because she can create life, while her own needs and boundaries are repeatedly ignored. The most disturbing thing to me is that the people who worship Him don’t even truly care about what they destroy. They can adore him while simultaneously destroying the very thing that makes his creation possible. And he allows it because their love and worship matter more to him than protecting Mother. Which brings me to the ending, where I just sat there thinking: What the actual fuck? Mother gives everything. She is destroyed. The house is destroyed. The cycle ends in complete devastation. And Him? He survives. He takes what remains and starts again. So we’re essentially watching a cycle where Mother is repeatedly created, used, worshipped only for what she can give, destroyed by the people who claim to love the Creator, and then replaced by another Mother so the cycle can continue. I understand that this is supposed to represent something much larger. I understand the biblical parallels. I understand the commentary on humanity, religion, creation, environmental destruction, and the endless cycle of worship and destruction. I still fucking hated it. I spent the entire movie waiting for someone to simply tell these people to leave the house. 😭 Maybe the allegory is brilliant. Maybe the symbolism is layered and intentional. Maybe there are dozens of things I could analyze about this movie. But as an actual viewing experience? I was miserable. I didn’t feel scared. I didn’t feel emotionally connected. I felt increasingly irritated at a man who couldn’t respect his wife’s privacy, increasingly uncomfortable watching a group of people turn into a cult around him, and increasingly horrified by the realization that nobody seemed to care about Mother as a person. One & half stars. I understand you, mother!. I just don’t like you. 💀

texto: Dans la catégorie des films que j’aurais jamais regardés de moi même mais que j’ai vus parce qu’ils passaient à la télé, Mother! c’est celui auquel je pense le plus. Je le prends comme un film d’auteur qui cherche à dire un truc de très vrai mais qui le fait par la recherche d’impact tellement dérangeant que ça dessert l’œuvre. Au fond, c’est l’histoire d’un écrivain qui voue sa vie à l’écriture de son livre, et qui une fois publié le regarde être disséqué, analysé, jugé par le public qui ne connaît pas la personne qui l’a écrit, seulement le produit fini. La mère qui donne naissance à son bébé, et qui invite des parfaits inconnus pour célébrer sa naissance, et les inconnus se mettent à fouiller les placards, à faire comme chez eux, et a un moment le bébé tombe par terre et les gens mangent le bébé - Stop. Y’a des trucs qu’on fait pas. On met pas en scène un bébé qui se fait dévorer par une foule de sauvages. Et pourtant, si j’en crois le film, je fais donc partie de ces gens qui piétinent sa création. Mais il y a une difference entre faire comprendre qu’on saccage sa création et montrer un nourrisson se faire déchiqueter par une foule sous les yeux de sa mère impuissante et de son père qui refuse d’agir Et à l’époque quand j’ai vu ça, ça m’a carrément énervé. Comment ça y’a un studio qui met en scène un truc comme ça et ça sort en salles et c’est acclamé par le public? On touche pas les bébés. Y’a des limites. Pour moi c’est de la branlette intellectuelle d’auteur. Si tu veux faire du sensationnel, fais confiance à ton public au lieu d’aller chercher dans un registre aussi malsain.

texto: Je trouve ça dommage de faire un huis clos pour y mettre tous les éléments de l'extérieur tels qu'ils sont. Par exemple une manif, la guerre, la police ? Dans une maison ? J'ai adoré la première partie, la tension est extrêmement forte, la mise en scène est vraiment plaisante, il y a un vrai jeu entre des plans très serrés et des plans en pdv subjectif plus larges. Ça donne une impression de voyeurisme, comme si la femme et la maison était la même personne (ce qui est le but). Ensuite il y a les premiers invités (la famille nucléaire), cette tension continue et en même temps des mystères se développent : qui sont ils ? Que se passe-t-il au sous sol ? Que signifie cette pierre ? Qu'écrit le mari ? C'est oppressant, on ne sait rien et tous les éléments sont stressants. À partir de ce moment là c'est très bien, les symboliques sont délicates, complètes et ça garde une forte puissance de propos. Personnellement j'y ai d'abord vu une idée féministe, la femme fait un travail monstrueux de rénovation pour que l'homme ait tout le buzz en écrivant (alors même qu'il écrit pas). Ensuite arrivent tout le reste de la famille, ça continue d'être stressant mais ça en devient ironique. C'est à dire qu'avant on savait que ça pouvait déraper puisqu'il y a avait un petit groupe d'intrus, mais là avec un groupe de 20 personnes, toutes différentes, la seule peur qui reste c'est la gêne qu'on ressent face à leurs comportements. Après que tout cela se calme, on revient sur du bon contenu : la relation dans le couple. Puis suite à la révélation de la grossesse et la fin de l'écriture, tout repars en couilles. Mais cette fois si c'est pire puisque plus rien n'a de symbolique. L'intérêt du début c'est surtout qu'il y a une symbolique cachée qui est la genèse de la bible. Mais passé cette étape là, on se lance dans une critique du christianisme d'une manière grossière. Pourquoi ne pas continuer le jeu de la symbolique ? Pourquoi faire des évènements aussi burlesques ? C'est vraiment de plus en plus grossier, tout ça pour avoir une critique très mid style "ah ouais la bible dit de tout partager, d'être gentil avec son prochain mais les gens ils sont pas gentils boubouuh 😣"  ou sinon une critique un peu incompréhensible qui est que Dieu ce flocko il veut trop la fame. Mouais à revoir. En plus le propos féministe que j'ai expliqué avant est bien estompé puisque ce n'est pas vraiment la femme qui charbonne (dans les 2 sens du terme) mais c'est Dieu qui crée Marie (la maison) comme hôte afin d'accueillir Jésus pendant qu'il écrit. C'est à dire qu'elle ne travaille pas vrm, c'est elle la maison et elle se prépare juste à son rôle premier : accoucher de l'autre pelo à l'auréole. Au global, le film avait un potentiel de fou, mais on ne sait pourquoi c'est passé du thriller horrifique à du comique.

Hang in there for this bonus effect - especially if you were into the movie.

texto: Фильмы Даррена Аронофски надо чувствовать, а не смотреть. Они как голые провода заряженные чистыми эмоциями. В «мама!» они ещё и религиозно подкованные. Намёки на суть происходящего зрителю даются сразу же, в первые минуты. Здесь каждый элемент дома, не говоря о самом доме — метафора. Раковина — это ни что не иное, как закреплённый божий закон, а ебанутые гости – люди, и грехопадение Евы. К середине фильм уже перестаёт дурить зрителя и открывает свои настоящие чакры и мотивации, по полной устраивая настоящий апокалипсис. Он — уже нечто иное, как деятельность человека на земле, ужатое до размеров одного дома. Имя «поэт», само за себя говорит. Под конец, фильм даёт понять две вещи: муза не вечна, а создатель - ненасытен. Мы, люди, можем не усугублять, и в мире провести отведенный нам срок, но мы всегда будет ненасытны в своих желаниях и нам всегда будет мало. Такова человеческая природа. Фильм ахуенно показал агонию умирающего человечества, и это — бесспорно!

texto: Very disturbing introduction to Aronofsky. This had a really strong first hour, that for me tapered off as it progressed. The atmosphere was well done, sort of established a dream-like state that made the bizarre escalation of events not seem too far fetched. Mostly felt like this was done through all of the characters interactions being very distant to mother, with an emphasis on her husband. Nobody’s really responding or registering with her actual dialogue - really isolated Lawrence as the only grounded character, super terrifying when taking into account the husband is her only lifeline in the setting and he quickly shows he is not reliable. This, as well these long panning shots of mother claustrophobically close to the camera attempting to maneuver her home (in which continuity seems to only apply where she is present) make it super nightmarish. Was super off trying to analyze this movie, first half felt more like a psyche thriller and I thought these visiting characters were representing all aspects of doubt in her life, like the man challenging her autonomy over the home and decision making while the women challenges her adequacy as a wife and potential mother - the sons would just be some internal violence I guess? Came around to the biblical allegory thing but I think my original outlook tainted the way the rest of the film panned out. Solid overall.

texto: Uma das obras mais densas que eu já vi. Tal qual experimentar um prato que de tão spicy deixa a sua boca adormecida, e mesmo assim você curte a experiência, Mother não é filme pra você sair tranquilo, é pesado, espesso, um turbilhão que te deixa cansado. Eu pessoalmente nunca fui masoquista que gosta de sofrer com algo que era pra me trazer júbilo, mas Darren Aronofsky acaba por me fazer senti prazer em ver algo pertubador. Caim, Abel, Adão, Eva, Cristo, Mãe, A humanidade, todos esses são muito bem retratados, mas estão simplesmente ofuscador por Javier Bardem, um ególatra maluco que interpreta Deus, só fica a pergunta de: como ele consegue ser tão perfeito na própria visão, e mesmo assim ser a pior coisa da existência?

texto: As a huge Napoleon fan, I was really excited to watch this movie, and I honestly had pretty high expectations. The costumes were probably my favorite part. They looked beautiful, were mostly historically accurate, and I loved how they recreated so many scenes from famous paintings. Those moments really made it feel like history had come to life.What disappointed me was the story. I really wish they had shown more of Napoleon’s childhood and his rise to power because I think that would have made him feel like a much more complex and sympathetic character. Instead, the movie jumps around a lot and never really lets you understand who he was as a person.It also felt stuck somewhere between a documentary and a historical drama. It wasn’t accurate enough to work as a documentary since so many scenes and events were clearly imagined or changed, but at the same time it wasn’t entertaining enough to make up for those changes. I kept waiting to become emotionally invested, but it never really happened. It looks impressive, but I left feeling like it had missed the chance to tell the incredible story of one of history’s most fascinating people.

texto: Długo wzbraniałem się przed nadrobieniem "Napoleona". Najlepsze lata Ridleya Scotta już dawno przeminęły, a w międzyczasie trudno było uniknąć opinii, że nie do końca ten film zasłużonemu reżyserowi wyszedł, ale mimo wszystko podszedłem do niego z czystą głową. Początek wzniecił sporo nadziei swoimi przedstawionymi w sposób imponujący i brutalny scenami batalistycznymi, które poziomu nie obniżyły już do samego końca i były najjaśniejszym punktem filmu. Co zaś momentalnie stanęło w kontrze do pozytywów to sam pomysł na przedstawienie głównego bohatera, gdzie Scott nie potrafił się zdecydować czy chce ukazać go w sposób karykaturalny, czy też jako pomysłowego i brutalnego przywódcę. Na tym przede wszystkim ucierpiał, pomimo swojego kunsztu aktorskiego, Joaquin Phoenix. Generalnie można stwierdzić, że twórcy nie do końca zapanowali nad tą produkcją, bo kilka dziwnych i niezrozumiałych zabiegów można znaleźć również w montażu. Co jednak najbardziej kłuje w oczy, to to jak poszatkowana i pozbawiona jakiejkolwiek ciągłości jest tu fabuła. Przez większość czasu nic się tutaj nie spina, a widz zamiast starannie opowiedzianej historii, dostaje zbiór najważniejszych momentów z życia Bonaparte. Żeby nie kończyć swoich przemyśleń tak ponuro, dodam że Vanessa Kirby świetnie się odnalazła w roli Józefiny. Szkoda, bo był potencjał.

texto: Al ser una pelicula sobre la historia de Nápoleon le tenía una gran expectativa pero me decepcionó un montón por las carencias que tuvo por todos lados. Para empezar no me podes poner a alguien conocido como intérprete de una figura histórica, en estas películas a mi gusto tenes que poner a un actor que no lo conozca ni su vieja incluso si eso implica bajar la calidad actoral, porque uno después cuando la ve, no está viendo a Napoleón, está viendo a Joaquín Phoenix y que te pase eso es que se te cague toda la película. En términos cinematográficos me pareció buena en las escenas de batallas, pero de las 4 que muestran 2 las mostraron en menos de 10 segundos entonces lo interesante que tiene te deja con gusto a poco, después el resto de las escenas me parecen básicas, no creo que Joaquín Phoenix le haya agregado mucha calidad o personalidad al personaje. Para lo que pudo haber hecho, que Ridley Scott haga esto es para que lo descarten en un río. Habiendo hablado de esas dos cosas, una de las mayores carencias de la película sino la mayor es el tiempo que se toman y el cómo retratan la relación de él con Josephine, habrá tomado sin exagerar mitad de las 2:30 que tiene la película y es lo que menos importa de toda su historia, aparte de que las escenas son cualquiera mal, no se hablo de un solo General que después de las batallas en sí, debe ser lo más relevante de contar: no profundizaron con Murat, no hablaron ni de Davout ni de Ney y más grave todavía no hablaron nada de Lannes, a Dumas lo mostraron forzado solo por ser su único general negro y lo hicieron con errores históricos como que era amigo medio íntimo cuando no era para nada el caso o que apareciera después de la campaña de Egipto cuando en realidad creo que ni había terminado esa campaña que ya se había retirado. La crítica de las campañas seguro debe ser la que más la habrán hecho y con razón, ya que es realmente increíble lo escaso que está en material de las campañas que es los más importante y lo único que debería tener en mente el director al hacer la película ya que justamente las campañas son lo que le dieron peso a su figura, hasta incluso más que las batallas de nombre aisladas. En la campaña de Italia mostraron la de Toulon por arriba y después nada más, en la de egypto no se mostró una sola  batalla ni siquiera lo que pasó cuando se exilio y dejó a Kleber. Mas adelante se pueden saltear alguna que otra batalla pero siempre y cuando se mantenga el hilo de la historia, cosa que no pasó, el que no pispeo la historia antes de verla no hay forma de que se ubique porque no se entiende nada. texto: The year is 2023, and two new biopics have been released about some of the most destructive men known to our world. One of those films is named Oppenheimer, and it clocks in at roughly three hours and one minute. The other film is named Napoleon, and it clocks in at roughly two hours and thirty-eight minutes. Now ask yourself: Which film is longer? If you answered Oppenheimer, then you haven’t watched both films. After a rewatch the film decidedly conveys its points a lot better, and it’s a decent biopic that separates the man from the myth. That being said, decent is the word for it, because half of the time either Joaquin’s acting is meandering and aimless or Napoleon’s mood is being written to abruptly shift contradictory to how he should be acting. The one highlight of Napoleon’s writing is it at least shows the slow degradation of the main character’s mannerisms as they get overtaken by ambition. For anyone wondering, yes I have watched Oppenheimer before and yes at some point I will rewatch it and rate it accordingly. Anyways that’s it; no need to drag this review out in the way Napoleon drags out its runtime.

texto: Como diría el grandísimo PEPO FANTASY: “en plan… se centran demasiado en lo que es el amor con la jamba”. Me da realmente pena no haber caído de pie viendo ‘Napoleon’ y que no haya conseguido embaucarme en su viaje por la vida del gobernante corso más allá de por la calidad y espectacularidad de las escenas bélicas que son por lo que realmente sí que merece la pena ver esta película en el cine. Una decepción más de mi queridísimo Ridley Scott que vuelve a traer una película visual y sonoramente muy llamativa pero que deja que desear en cuanto a trama y personajes (sobre todo teniendo en cuenta que no es un personaje cualquiera si no una de las personas más influyentes de la historia). Y a esto hay que sumarle que la decepción que te llevas es doble cuando vas a ver una película con un director como este y que protagoniza ni mas ni menos que the one and only Joaquin Phoenix. Sin poder (obviamente) definir su actuación como mala o mediocre, hay algo en ella que no me ha convencido, sin saber realmente si ha sido por la actuación en sí o por la cantidad de grandes papeles que asocio a este actor y que por ello me cueste más verle en la piel de un personaje tan tan conocido. Una trama repleta de saltos y que, pese a narrar todos los hechos importantes de la vida de Napoleón, lo hace de una forma que en ciertos momentos es capaz de sacarme de la película por su velocidad para pasar de unos sucesos a otros, por la ausencia de elementos clave (Trafalgar) y por el, para mi gusto, exceso de trama dedicada al amor; aunque la actuación de Vanessa Kirby sea bastante bastante GOAT.

texto: I've always thought that making a film about a great historical figure is one of the hardest things a director can do. Unless it's a TV series or a whole film saga, trying to fit an entire life into a single movie means leaving out a lot of important moments. And when that person is Napoleon Bonaparte—a man whose life was defined by politics, military genius, and an incredibly complex personality—the challenge becomes even greater. Any filmmaker has to balance historical accuracy with cinematic spectacle, and I think Ridley Scott only partially succeeds. The film follows the major milestones of Napoleon's life in chronological order and recreates some of his most famous campaigns. At the same time, it takes several dramatic liberties to make them more visually impressive. The cannon fire aimed at the Pyramids never happened, Napoleon wasn't present at Marie Antoinette's execution, and the famous frozen lake sequence at Austerlitz is a huge exaggeration of what actually took place. Those scenes are entertaining, but they prioritize spectacle over history. Honestly, those changes don't bother me that much because they're based on real events that have simply been dramatized. What I do miss are the omissions that make it harder to understand who Napoleon really was. The film barely touches on his background as a member of the Corsican minor nobility, something that was essential in allowing him to attend military school in France and begin the career that eventually led him to become Emperor. Joséphine also deserved a more nuanced portrayal. The movie mostly reduces her role to Napoleon's wife and his desperate need for an heir. While that was certainly an important part of their relationship, she was also a politically influential figure who navigated the highest circles of French society and played a significant role while Napoleon was away. The film turns a remarkably capable historical figure into little more than a romantic subplot. That said, I do think the movie succeeds in portraying Napoleon as more than just a military genius. We see an awkward, emotionally intense man whose love for Joséphine shapes much of his personal life. Joaquin Phoenix captures that contradiction between the vulnerable individual and the unstoppable conqueror surprisingly well. I also liked how the film hints at Napoleon's admiration for Julius Caesar and Alexander the Great. At times, Scott presents him as someone driven by an almost classical sense of duty—a man convinced that his destiny was to serve France above everything else. Whether intentional or not, that echoes the Roman ideal of devotion to the state and adds another layer to his character.

texto: I’ll preface by saying i only watched the director’s cut. That said, god, i hate that i liked this. Do i think it’s a good portrayal of how Napoleon was perceived by others? Perhaps not, but i do think it does a fantastic job in making you feel like how it would’ve been inside his mind throughout his life. Especially towards the end where failure was more and more common. The huge battles, sets, cavalry charges, all of it was a feast for the eyes. texto: I've always thought that making a film about a great historical figure is one of the hardest things a director can do. Unless it's a TV series or a whole film saga, trying to fit an entire life into a single movie means leaving out a lot of important moments. And when that person is Napoleon Bonaparte—a man whose life was defined by politics, military genius, and an incredibly complex personality—the challenge becomes even greater. Any filmmaker has to balance historical accuracy with cinematic spectacle, and I think Ridley Scott only partially succeeds. The film follows the major milestones of Napoleon's life in chronological order and recreates some of his most famous campaigns. At the same time, it takes several dramatic liberties to make them more visually impressive. The cannon fire aimed at the Pyramids never happened, Napoleon wasn't present at Marie Antoinette's execution, and the famous frozen lake sequence at Austerlitz is a huge exaggeration of what actually took place. Those scenes are entertaining, but they prioritize spectacle over history. Honestly, those changes don't bother me that much because they're based on real events that have simply been dramatized. What I do miss are the omissions that make it harder to understand who Napoleon really was. The film barely touches on his background as a member of the Corsican minor nobility, something that was essential in allowing him to attend military school in France and begin the career that eventually led him to become Emperor. Joséphine also deserved a more nuanced portrayal. The movie mostly reduces her role to Napoleon's wife and his desperate need for an heir. While that was certainly an important part of their relationship, she was also a politically influential figure who navigated the highest circles of French society and played a significant role while Napoleon was away. The film turns a remarkably capable historical figure into little more than a romantic subplot. That said, I do think the movie succeeds in portraying Napoleon as more than just a military genius. We see an awkward, emotionally intense man whose love for Joséphine shapes much of his personal life. Joaquin Phoenix captures that contradiction between the vulnerable individual and the unstoppable conqueror surprisingly well. I also liked how the film hints at Napoleon's admiration for Julius Caesar and Alexander the Great. At times, Scott presents him as someone driven by an almost classical sense of duty—a man convinced that his destiny was to serve France above everything else. Whether intentional or not, that echoes the Roman ideal of devotion to the state and adds another layer to his character.

texto: This cut is so much better than the original. While I was planning to save Ridley Scott’s Napoleon until I reached the next chapter of my director deep dive, the opportunity arose to watch it, so I took it. At three and a half hours, Scott’s director’s cut is a substantial expansion of the theatrical version. It doesn’t quite add the sense of scale I expected from an extra hour of runtime, but that’s easy to forgive when the film delivers on the level that it does. Napoleon certainly has its flaws, and some of them are significant, but in the grand scheme of things, it’s a great time. From the opening sequence, the film radiates a grit that seems to seep off the screen, steadily building throughout the runtime. That escalation culminates in several disturbing scenes of political violence that are incredibly effective. Scott captures the messiness of government, revolution, and monarchy with remarkable clarity, making it easy to understand the absolute chaos of France’s political climate during this period. The director’s cut is far more expansive and patient with its pacing, allowing these elements to breathe and making the atmosphere all the more effective. Much of that atmosphere is still rooted in the relationship between Josephine and Napoleon, just as it was in the original cut. What elevates it here are the expanded plotlines surrounding Napoleon’s rise to power, along with the greater focus given to key political and historical developments. These additions provide the film with far more depth and substance than its theatrical counterpart. My biggest issue with the film, both the director’s cut and the theatrical version, is its use of American accents in place of French ones. It’s a truly baffling decision that repeatedly pulls the viewer out of the film’s otherwise immersive atmosphere. It feels especially strange when you have a Russian character speaking with a Russian accent while a native Frenchman speaks with an American one. It constantly distracted me. I understand why Joaquin Phoenix was cast, he is excellent and perfectly suited to the role in many ways. However, I can’t understand why he doesn’t attempt a French accent at all. While his star power undoubtedly helped the film commercially, the decision to forgo an accent altogether may have avoided certain pitfalls, but it ultimately hurts the film’s authenticity and integrity.

texto: Après 2 films, j'ai du mal à me positionner sur le cinéma de Sciamma. Je trouve évidemment que celui-ci est bien plus abouti que Bande de filles , mais je dois avouer qu'aucune scène ne m'a réellement emporté. Beaucoup de maladresses dans le montage, notamment cette célèbre scène autour du feu qui est un bel exemple. La scène est super puissante grâce aux chants et au décor, mais elle se finit prématurément par un raccord très prévisible et forcé. Au final, la thématique, le scénario et le jeu des actrices ne sont pas suffisamment soutenus par la mise en scène et par les choix de plans que je trouve globalement peu signifiants. Ça reste un super film qui s'affranchit totalement du regard masculin, avec une grande cohérence visuelle grâce à la peinture

I can’t deny the acting there was beautiful and tragic.

texto: I have nothing intelligent to say about this film, not even anything I can disguise as intelligence. All I have is what I thought while watching, which consisted mostly of the thinking equivalent of an eye roll, or a scoff, maybe. When I am watching a film, the defining factor for me—which is a defining factor which builds the basis of “good art,” for me—is whether or not it invokes emotions, & if it does, what kinds of emotions? The amount of symbolism a film saturates itself w/, (this film includes color theory, metaphors, eroticism, babies, & whatnots) does not make it inherently better. Maybe it becomes more interesting in its conversations concerning itself, but it does not, in my opinion, make the film “better.” Rather, I think, a good film is good when it can (a) express emotions about humanity, & (b) do it in an interesting way(do not confuse interesting w/ lots of symbolism). This film does, in my opinion, does not stir emotion, & I didn’t find it particularly interesting in its expressions. For me, if a film has bad dialogue, it really turns me off of it, in terms of my interest in it, which I hope doesn’t make me sound pretentious, but this film didn’t have good dialogue, or rather, it didn’t have dialogue that I enjoyed. Most of the film just felt like one character asking another character a question, & the other says “Oui,” or “No,” & then they make eyes at each other for a solid thirty seconds. Those are the parts that, to me, felt the most hokey. Also, I thought that the characters were very melodramatic, which you could argue is because they’re two gay women experiencing love for the first time, but I feel like that’s just an excuse for bad writing. It’s possible to portray lesbian romances w/o making the characters act totally melodramatic(Desert Hearts & The Handmaiden are two that come to mind w/ my extremely lmtd knowledge). There were some parts I liked. I liked the part where she reads the myth of Orpheus. I thought the abortion scene was very well done(I thought Sophie was a very well done character in general). I like that there were no men in the film, because, like, to put men on the island would totally desacralize it. I like the final scene, with the music performance. &c. Not to mention that—& I know this might be totally solipsistic of me to say—the subjects that the film focus on aren’t exactly in my ball park of experiences, which usually isn’t the case for me. I really enjoyed Paris is Burning, but I’m not a drag queen; I love Allen Ginsberg’s Howl, even though I’m not a gay man in the ‘50s; so why do those pieces of art speak to me even though the experiences are foreign. I think it has something to do w/ those pieces being something more like timeless that this film really isn’t, I guess. If you read this far, I’m sorry.

texto: I have nothing intelligent to say about this film, not even anything I can disguise as intelligence. All I have is what I thought while watching, which consisted mostly of the thinking equivalent of an eye roll, or a scoff, maybe. When I am watching a film, the defining factor for me—which is a defining factor which builds the basis of “good art,” for me—is whether or not it invokes emotions, & if it does, what kinds of emotions? The amount of symbolism a film saturates itself w/, (this film includes color theory, metaphors, eroticism, babies, & whatnots) does not make it inherently better. Maybe it becomes more interesting in its conversations concerning itself, but it does not, in my opinion, make the film “better.” Rather, I think, a good film is good when it can (a) express emotions about humanity, & (b) do it in an interesting way(do not confuse interesting w/ lots of symbolism). This film does, in my opinion, does not stir emotion, & I didn’t find it particularly interesting in its expressions. For me, if a film has bad dialogue, it really turns me off of it, in terms of my interest in it, which I hope doesn’t make me sound pretentious, but this film didn’t have good dialogue, or rather, it didn’t have dialogue that I enjoyed. Most of the film just felt like one character asking another character a question, & the other says “Oui,” or “No,” & then they make eyes at each other for a solid thirty seconds. Those are the parts that, to me, felt the most hokey. Also, I thought that the characters were very melodramatic, which you could argue is because they’re two gay women experiencing love for the first time, but I feel like that’s just an excuse for bad writing. It’s possible to portray lesbian romances w/o making the characters act totally melodramatic(Desert Hearts & The Handmaiden are two that come to mind w/ my extremely lmtd knowledge). There were some parts I liked. I liked the part where she reads the myth of Orpheus. I thought the abortion scene was very well done(I thought Sophie was a very well done character in general). I like that there were no men in the film, because, like, to put men on the island would totally desacralize it. I like the final scene, with the music performance. &c. Not to mention that—& I know this might be totally solipsistic of me to say—the subjects that the film focus on aren’t exactly in my ball park of experiences, which usually isn’t the case for me. I really enjoyed Paris is Burning, but I’m not a drag queen; I love Allen Ginsberg’s Howl, even though I’m not a gay man in the ‘50s; so why do those pieces of art speak to me even though the experiences are foreign. I think it has something to do w/ those pieces being something more like timeless that this film really isn’t, I guess. If you read this far, I’m sorry.

Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019) Directed by Céline Sciamma Rating: 10 / 10 | Masterpiece ​Portrait of a Lady on Fire brought me to tears. It is a masterpiece that transcends usual romantic boundaries and clichés, burning down the traditional rules of the genre to create a love story that feels entirely, breathtakingly new. It starts on an isolated island, where a talented artist named Marianne (Noémie Merlant) is commissioned for a nearly impossible task: to paint the wedding portrait of Héloïse (Adèle Haenel), a young woman fiercely resisting her impending arranged marriage. Because Héloïse refuses to pose, Marianne must act as a walking companion by day, clandestinely stealing forbidden glances to memorize her subject's features to paint by night. What begins as a tense game of observation slowly ignites into a smoldering slow-burn of impossible yearning. As their walls crumble, the act of looking transforms into an explosive, deeply reciprocal romance with a devastatingly clear end. Director Céline Sciamma delivers something miraculous by entirely eliminating the male gaze. She actively strips away traditional power dynamics, ensuring the leads are on exact equal footing. The chemistry between Noémie Merlant and Adèle Haenel is electric; their bond, much like the portrait itself, is profoundly collaborative. But Sciamma’s boldest, most brilliant choice is the absence of a manipulative score. She packs every single frame with tangible emotion relying purely on Claire Mathon's luscious, warm cinematography and the visceral, ambient sounds of crashing waves and breathing. It is not just your love story. It explains the crushing tragedy of memory and the inevitability of loss. It brilliantly weaves in the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, challenging us to understand the difference between making the "lover's choice" and the "poet's choice." Haunted by the ghost of their sizzling final farewell, the film teaches us a brutal truth: the perfect song seldom plays during our most formative moments, and the perfect person seldom enters our lives at the right time. But choosing to remember them keeps the fire blazing long after the romance ends. It is really a gorgeous, devastatingly heartbreaking, and genuinely might be one of the best films I have ever seen. It is a story that is uniquely lesbian at its core, yet its profound meditation on the sting of lost love makes it starkly, beautifully universal. The final, unbroken shot of this movie is quite simply one of the greatest endings in cinematic history. • Resonance / Impact: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ • Cinematography / Visuals: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ • Acting / Performance: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ • Direction: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ • Soundtrack / Score: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ • Plot / Storytelling: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ Final Rating: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ When you're observing me, who do you think I'm observing?

texto: We did a spin-off, and I ended up with Portrait of a Lady on Fire. I went into this movie completely blind. I didn't know anything about it. The first thing that caught me was how visually appealing it is. Cinematically, I can absolutely see why people praise this movie so much. The cinematography, the framing, the performances, and the overall presentation are beautiful. The story is about two women and the relationship that develops between them. I understood what the movie was trying to say, and I could see the depth of their connection. I've also seen people call this one of the most perfect romances ever made, and some even compared its emotional impact to Titanic. But honestly, it didn't hit me that way. For me, I was watching it as a movie rather than emotionally placing myself inside the relationship. Even during the final moments, when people say the movie becomes extremely emotional, I was honestly just thinking, "How long is this going to take?" That doesn't mean I think the movie is bad. Quite the opposite. I think it's an excellent film from a cinematic perspective, and I'm glad I explored something completely different. I believe this is also my first French movie. But emotionally, it just wasn't for me. Maybe I'm simply not someone who connects strongly with romantic stories, and I've never personally experienced being in love, so perhaps that's one reason I couldn't connect with the relationship on that deeper level. 3.5/5

texto: Such an extraordinarily tender film, so slow and gentle, yet without a single second feeling wasted. One particularly striking aspect of this film is the use of silence and ambient sound. Early on this silence feels repressive, almost choking at times. Sound and music is used sparingly, but when it is present it is extremely cathartic. Waves violently breaking on the cliffs allow stolen glances, piano music welcomes brief closeness and intimacy, the thumping of cards brings shared laughter, the drone and sweet hum of the singing crowd a mutual look of tender understanding. Even in their first kiss the silence is too overpowering. However Marianne and Héloïse gradually break down that silence together until it bursts asunder, although not through violent noise, but instead a new silence, not repressive but intimate. Yet still they know that what they have must be fleeting and at times that very silence becomes suppressive, even oppressive, again. Together by the roaring waves they can be real, genuine, together. But not in the quiet false society. In a quiet moment Marianne has her look back, her last shared moment and goodbye. The storm has finally broken. The music at the end allows Héloïse a brief respite from the false life like she was told earlier it would, for her to feel and love and remember, her moments to escape from a society where they cannot be together. I am also a sucker for anything Orpheus and Eurydice related, and I believe this film to be one of the most interesting interpretations of the myth. Beautifully heartbreaking and heartbreakingly beautiful.

texto: What I love most is how the film tackles patriarchy without ever turning its ideas into speeches. It builds its argument through the way Marianne and Héloïse look at each other, paint each other, and gradually learn to exist as equals. Marianne first observes Héloïse in secret, treating her almost like an object to be studied and reproduced. "If you look at me, who do I look at?" Héloïse reveals that she has been learning Marianne’s gestures just as closely as Marianne has studied hers. The woman being painted has her own gaze, her own interpretation. Being seen becomes mutual, and equality begins when the observer accepts that she, too, is being observed. Consent changes the portrait in the same way. The first painting fails because it is made through secrecy and convention. Once she agrees to pose, the portrait becomes collaborative. Their love may ultimately be constrained by a patriarchal society that has already decided what Héloïse's future should look like, but the relationship itself refuses those same rules. It is built on reciprocity, consent, and recognition rather than possession. And when physical togetherness becomes impossible, art and memory preserve what society could not accommodate, not as a substitute for the life they might have shared, but as proof that it existed and permanently changed them. Patriarchy can dictate the shape of Héloïse's public life, but it cannot completely control how she loved, what she remembers, or the part of herself that survives in Marianne's art.

texto: This movie is an artistic ode to feminism and love • pure and genuine love that has no gender. With a complete absence of men throughout the film other than the last scene, it follows the beautiful story of a painter, a young woman called Hélöise, and her maid, Sofia. With building tension, emotional progression and throughout the most magnificent cinematography it portrays love at its most pure form and teaches us that it takes two to be funny. Hélöise is the lady on fire, Eyridice, and Marianne is Orpheus. It’s quite a foreshadowing, through this Ancient Greek myth, that these two women will eventually have to separate and be left only with the tender memory of each other. They were both the painters and the canvases to each other, slowly developing their emotions and interaction, creating dynamically this portrait together, the ultimate conviction of Hélöise, yet the occasion that prompted this tragic love story. And when I say tragic , I mean that these two were never meant to be together. And when it comes to the question “being free is being alone?” , the answer is no, being free is women helping women and making masterpieces like this.

Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019) Directed by Céline Sciamma Rating: 10 / 10 | Masterpiece ​Portrait of a Lady on Fire brought me to tears. It is a masterpiece that transcends usual romantic boundaries and clichés, burning down the traditional rules of the genre to create a love story that feels entirely, breathtakingly new. It starts on an isolated island, where a talented artist named Marianne (Noémie Merlant) is commissioned for a nearly impossible task: to paint the wedding portrait of Héloïse (Adèle Haenel), a young woman fiercely resisting her impending arranged marriage. Because Héloïse refuses to pose, Marianne must act as a walking companion by day, clandestinely stealing forbidden glances to memorize her subject's features to paint by night. What begins as a tense game of observation slowly ignites into a smoldering slow-burn of impossible yearning. As their walls crumble, the act of looking transforms into an explosive, deeply reciprocal romance with a devastatingly clear end. Director Céline Sciamma delivers something miraculous by entirely eliminating the male gaze. She actively strips away traditional power dynamics, ensuring the leads are on exact equal footing. The chemistry between Noémie Merlant and Adèle Haenel is electric; their bond, much like the portrait itself, is profoundly collaborative. But Sciamma’s boldest, most brilliant choice is the absence of a manipulative score. She packs every single frame with tangible emotion relying purely on Claire Mathon's luscious, warm cinematography and the visceral, ambient sounds of crashing waves and breathing. It is not just your love story. It explains the crushing tragedy of memory and the inevitability of loss. It brilliantly weaves in the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, challenging us to understand the difference between making the "lover's choice" and the "poet's choice." Haunted by the ghost of their sizzling final farewell, the film teaches us a brutal truth: the perfect song seldom plays during our most formative moments, and the perfect person seldom enters our lives at the right time. But choosing to remember them keeps the fire blazing long after the romance ends. It is really a gorgeous, devastatingly heartbreaking, and genuinely might be one of the best films I have ever seen. It is a story that is uniquely lesbian at its core, yet its profound meditation on the sting of lost love makes it starkly, beautifully universal.
